en: The Chronicle of the Three Jewels Through the Dynasties, Volume One: Imperial Chronology (Zhou and Qin).
Submitted by the Subject Fei Changfang, Academician for the Translation of Scriptures, during the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Northern Zhou.

Imperial Chronology (Zhou and Qin): Regarding the term "Imperial Chronology," this describes the birth of the Tathāgata in the kingdom of Śīna (India), corresponding to the Jiayi era of this land of Zhendan (China).
This was the time of the Zhou dynasty.
As the years have gradually receded and human generations have become disparate,
it is easy to become utterly confused regarding what precedes and follows when pointing to specific events.
Now, first in the upper volume, I shall trace the thread of the *gengzi* cycle from antiquity to the present;
in the lower volume, I shall continue the imperial chronology to provide a framework for the eras.
In this way, the succession of abdication and the rise of hegemonic lords will be as clear as a mirror before one's eyes.
The changes of markets and capitals are as clear as one’s own palm;
thereafter, examining the kings and lords whose grace covered all and who supported the destiny of the age,
we see that the Dharma of the Buddha flowed forth in accordance with the times, responding to capacities and saving sentient beings.
The interpretation of the sutras accords with the principles of the Confucian teachings, matching them as if by a hidden resonance.
It may truly be said that spiritual power descended from the Five Heavens and auspicious signs reached throughout the Nine Provinces.
When the mother of Ji Chang, Si, dreamed of a great man, she conceived and gave birth to Chang because of this inspiration.
He had the countenance of a dragon and eyebrows like tigers; his height was one zhang, and he possessed four breasts upon his chest.
His kingdom bordered the Western Rong tribes.
His governance extended eastward;
a vermilion phoenix descended as an auspicious omen,
and he changed the title of his reign to Zhou.
He was posthumously titled King Wen.
He established his capital at Feng and collected the remains of the deceased for burial;
thus all under heaven submitted and were won over.
Therefore, the Master said:
"How magnificent was the virtue of King Wen!
Without moving, he transformed all."
When his son Fa ascended the throne as King Wu and campaigned against Zhou,
he moved the capital to Haojing;
on the road, he encountered a man suffering from heat exhaustion, and he descended from his carriage to fan him.
He humbled himself before those of ten thousand chariots and cherished the myriad people as his own children.
Thus, Master Xunzi said:
"When King Wu was alive, the whole world sang his praises."
At his death, the four seas wept.

In the tenth year of the nineteenth sovereign, King Zhuang, which corresponds to the seventh year of Duke Zhuang in the Spring and Autumn Annals of Lu, on the night of the *xinmao* day in the fourth month of summer, the fixed stars were not visible.
In the middle of the night, stars fell like rain.

According to this, it was precisely at the time when the Tathāgata was born in the royal palace; however, the various virtuous sages of antiquity have offered differing estimations regarding the year of the Buddha’s birth, with some placing it earlier and others later.
According to the *Yifaxian zhuan*, by calculating the time of the Buddha’s birth, it was the twenty-sixth year of King Wuyi of the Yin dynasty, the year Jiawu.
From that time until the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, the year Dingyi, exactly one thousand six hundred and eighty-one years have passed.
According to the *Śramaṇadharma-śāstra* (依沙門法上) in response to inquiries from the kingdom of Goguryeo,
this corresponds to the twenty-fourth year of the reign of King Zhao (瑕), the fifth sovereign of the preceding Zhou dynasty, which was the Jia-yin year.
From that time until the present Ding-si year, one thousand four hundred and eighty-six years have elapsed.
Citing the *Mu Tianzi biezhuan* as evidence,
it states that Xiazi Man succeeded to the throne,
and King Mu heard that the Buddha was born in Kapilavastu.
He subsequently traveled westward and did not return.
According to the *Xiangzheng ji*, this occurred in the forty-eighth year of the reign of King Ping Yijiu, the seventeenth sovereign of the Eastern Zhou, which was the year Wuwu.
From that time until the present year, Dingyi, one thousand three hundred and twenty-three years have elapsed.
According to the calculations of the Later Zhou śramaṇa Shi Dao’an, based on the dates of Kumārajīva and the pillar inscription,
this corresponds to the fifth year of the reign of King Lin (Huan Wang), the eighteenth sovereign of the Former Zhou, which was the year of Yichou.
Up to the present year of Ding-si, it has been one thousand two hundred and twenty-five years.

This is calculated based on the records of the various sages after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, which Vāgbhū (Zhao Boxiu) obtained from Vinaya Master Hongdu at Mount Lu in the first year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty.
Thus, from the second year of King Liang’s reign— the twenty-ninth sovereign of the Eastern Zhou,
the Jiaxu year— until the present Dingyi year, it has been approximately one thousand six hundred and one years.
This alone is the most proximate [explanation].
According to the Tripiṭaka teachings and the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, it is asked:
Why did the Buddha not ordain women?
Out of reverence for the Dharma, the True Dharma was destined to endure for one thousand years;

however, because women were permitted to enter the order, it was reduced by five hundred years. By establishing the observance of the Eight Rules of Respect, it was restored to its full duration of one thousand years.
Thereafter, the Semblance Dharma shall also last for one thousand years,
and the Final Dharma for ten thousand years.
During five thousand years of this period, those who study shall attain the three types of supernormal knowledge as well as the four fruits of arhatship.
Six thousand years hence, one will study without attaining the Way.
Ten thousand years thereafter, the texts and characters of the scriptures will naturally perish and vanish;
there will remain only those who appear with shaved heads and wear the *kāṣāya*.
In the age of the True Dharma, the flavor of the Mahāyāna was pure and rich;
by the time of the Semblance Age, its flavor had diminished and become thin.
If one enters the Age of the Final Dharma, there will be no Mahāyāna at all.
It was improper for slaves to leave the household life and defile pure conduct;
it was improper for an evil king ruling the world to impose taxes upon monks and nuns.
Now, such things shall not occur.
Because the interaction between the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma has not yet been profound,
and the Three Jewels have flourished once more with the Mahāyāna widely disseminated,
how could one possibly be considered a successor to the Age of the Final Dharma?
Now, relying upon such scriptures as the *Lalitavistara* and the *Buddhacarita*, I have collated them with the records of the ancient sages.
Lightly citing a single corner of this vast subject, I respectfully present it to future sages,
hoping that the traces of the Sage may be proclaimed and entrusted to his skillful means (*upāya*).
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Gui-si, the ninth year of King Zhuang’s reign,

the Buddha manifested in the form of a white elephant and descended from Tuṣita Heaven into the right side of Queen Māyā, the principal consort of the Great King Śuddhodana, in the city of Kapilavastu in Central India.
At that time, the various devas secretly followed and protected him within the womb;
hidden from view, he was rarely known by the eyes of the world.
On the eighth day of the second month of the middle spring in the tenth year, at the hour when the lunar mansion of Preta (Ārdrā) was in conjunction.
He was born reclining on his right side beneath a *pāla* tree in the Lumbinī Garden.
Since the signs of his birth were thus manifest,
the *Samantaprabhāsa-sūtra* (*Puyao jing*) states:
He universally radiated great light that illuminated the three thousandfold world-system;
this is what is meant by the left-hand tradition’s statement that the fixed stars do not appear and the night is luminous.
The *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Ruiying jing*) states that the constellation Puṣya descended to appear and attend the birth of the Prince;
thus, the *Zuozhuan* records that "stars fell like rain."
The *Benxing jing* (Sūtra on Past Deeds) states that rain falls naturally from a cloudless sky;
Du’s commentary explains that this refers to a time when there are no clouds.
The *Zuozhuan* also states:
"It accompanies the rain.
However, the calendar of the Ji-Zhou dynasty takes the eleventh month as the first month.
What is referred to as the fourth month is actually the fifth day of the *xinmao* (ox-day) in the current second month;
thus, the records of the Lu Annals are erroneous.
The śramaṇa Dao’an composed the *Treatise on the Two Teachings* (*Erjiao lun*).
When calculated using the Jia calendar, it coincides exactly with the eighth day;
however, by taking the year of his birth as the year of his attainment of enlightenment,
the duration of the Buddha’s lifetime was consequently extended by thirty years.
In the seventh year of the first year of Emperor Xi’s reign, the Gengzi year, at age seven,
the Buddha traveled by ox-cart to the schoolhouse. In the tenth year of the fourth year, the Gui Mao year, at age ten,
he competed in feats of strength with his peers from the Śākya clan.
In the third year of King Hui, the Dingwei year, at the age of fourteen,
he accompanied his father the king on an excursion.
Upon exiting the eastern gate of the city, he saw a sick man and turned back.
In the sixth year, the gengxu year, at the age of seventeen,
he took Qiuyi as his consort.
In the eighth year, the renzi year, at the age of nineteen.
According to the *Shier you jing* (Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings), at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month, he left the city to renounce the household life;
the *Zengyi ahan jing*, fascicle twenty-four, states that the Buddha renounced the world at the age of twenty.
I was twenty-nine years old when I left the household life, desiring to deliver sentient beings.
It is also said:
At the age of twenty, he studied among the non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthikas).
The *Dīrgha Āgama* also states that he left the household life at the age of twenty-nine.
Inferring from these broad principles, the Tathāgata remained in the world for seventy-nine years.
If he left home at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five,
the time he spent transforming sentient beings would have been only forty-five years.
However, the *Dhyānārya-sūtra* states that Śākyamuni taught and transformed sentient beings with a single body for forty-nine years;
most other sūtras likewise state this.
He left home at nineteen;
this is now taken as the correct account.
If one were to claim he left home at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five, [it would be incorrect].
In the sūtras, there is very little mention;
it merely states that he studied among the non-Buddhists for twenty years.
This would mean that he attained the Way only after fifty years;
thus, one knows it is erroneous.
In the nineteenth year, the Guihai year, he was thirty.
On the eighth day of the second month, when the morning star appeared, he attained clear and perfect awakening and realized the Unsurpassed Way. *The Sutra on the Parinirvāṇa*, Scroll II.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
Since I attained the Way, the years have likewise reached forty-nine.
A Buddha is difficult to behold;
only once every one hundred and forty million years does Maitreya appear.
The *Chanyao* states:
"From the time the Tathāgata attained enlightenment until forty-nine years later,
this was of one single flavor."
The fifth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
The Buddha said to Subhadra,
"Since I attained Buddhahood fifty years ago— forty-nine years have passed— I have dwelt among the worlds of devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits."
He preached the Dharma and transformed beings, causing each to attain liberation and realize the four fruits of the path.
Those who turned back the flow of existence numbered as many as the sands of the Ganges;
those who escaped the three miserable realms and were reborn among devas or humans were beyond all calculation.
When the karmic conditions of sentient beings were exhausted,
on the night of the fifteenth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Kuang era (the Renzi year),
the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa at the city of Kuśinagara in Central India.
From that time until the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, the Ding-si year, one thousand two hundred and five years have passed;
according to both the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, the Eye of the World was extinguished on the fifteenth day of the second month.
The *Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb Sūtra* states:
"On the eighth day of the second month, he entered parinirvāṇa.
It further states:
The dates for his initial birth, attainment of the Way, and even his entry into nirvana are all the eighth day of the fourth month.
The ancient translations by former masters all state that these should instead be the second month.
The reason for this was that Rājagṛha was three thousand *li* from the city of Kauśāmbī;
it was seven days after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa before the cremation took place and the disciples finally dispersed.
Kāśyapa proceeded toward Rājagṛha for the summer retreat at the beginning of the rainy season to compile the Dharma-piṭaka.
The great assembly he had led—both the wise and the ignorant—arrived together at Rājagṛha, where they finally began the process of selection and verification.
It was not possible for [the Buddha] to arrive at his destination on that very day;
yet while other sūtras all state that he entered nirvāṇa at midnight,
only the *Sudharman-vinaya* alone says it was at dawn.
The sūtra explains that "extinction" (nirvāṇa) indicates a specific time;
it is intended to show sentient beings that they will be separated from the Buddha-sun.
It must be during the middle watch of the night or at the time of the first watch;
since it was not yet dawn,
this indicated that the subsequent Buddha would appear in the world only after a long interval.
If it is at midnight,
they are positioned at equal intervals;
by the time of the latter part of the night, [they appear as such].
Before long, the Buddha will appear;
it will be only when Maitreya has reached one billion years of age,
and furthermore, it will not be in a different kalpa.
The mid-night period is considered correct.

The king of Jambudvīpa was named Aśoka.
He ruled from Pāṭaliputra in Eastern India and collected the Buddha’s relics,
enshrining them in eighty-four thousand precious stupas scattered throughout the land.

In the kingdom of China, they exist everywhere—along the banks of the Yangtze and Han rivers, and from the Guanzhong region in the west to the eastern provinces.
At that time, it was the twenty-sixth year of King Jing’s reign in the Zhou dynasty, the year of Dingwei.
From King Wu to King Xian, there were thirty-nine kings over a period of eight hundred and eighty-four years.
They resided in four locations in total: Feng, Hao, Luoyi, and Chengzhou.
King Zhaoxiang of the Ying clan reigned for fifty-two years; he extinguished the Zhou and styled his state Qin.
He changed the capital of Haojing to Xianyang and continued to reside there as his seat of government.
Reaching the twenty-sixth year of the reign of the first Emperor, the First Sovereign,
he swept away the six states;

He divided the world into thirty-six commanderies.
In the thirty-fourth year, all existing classics were completely incinerated;
only medical prescriptions and pharmaceutical arts were not subject to the flames.
All of this was reduced to ashes.

the Jiǎwǔ year, there were nine hundred and thirty-three years and forty-two sovereigns in between.
The Zhou dynasty comprised sixteen kings over a period of four hundred and fifty-three years.
Prior to the appearance of the Buddha, these names were not recorded.
Starting from King Zhuang’s reign, when the Tathāgata was born into the world, until the beginning of the Han dynasty, the chronological years have been formally documented.
Twenty-six rulers presided for a total of four hundred and eighty-one years.

Regarding the "Imperial Years" (from Wei, Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, Zhou, and the Great Sui): from the Three Sovereigns (*sanhuang*), when Heaven had but one ruler, down to the Two Han dynasties, when the earth had no second minister.
From the Wei and Jin dynasties down to our Great Sui ruling the world,
the capital cities during this interval were as numerous as bristles on a hedgehog;
there were twenty-two states with capitals where crows perched and cranes stood.
The first group consists of Wu, San, Qin, Liang, Wei, Qi, Chen, and so forth.
Although these eight states each preserved their own cultural prestige,
they all engaged in the translation of Buddhist scriptures.
If one can cause the Three Jewels to endure and be maintained,
then the four modes of birth will receive their reliance and support;
thus, those who strive for goodness cause blessings to flow forth.
Consequently, the records of the world have been handed down in succession;
yet, regarding the catalogs of the *piṭakas*, there is no longer anything heard of them.
At that time, there were fourteen kingdoms ruled by hegemonies, none of which promoted the holy teachings.
Regarding these matters, there is no one who knows their ancestral origins or cultivation; now,
each shall rely on those historical records to briefly mark their dates and eras, so that the strengths and weaknesses,
as well as the beginnings and ends, the abandonments and prosperities, may be understood.
In the second year of the Huangchu era of Emperor Wen of the Cao Wei dynasty, the year of Xinchou (220 CE),
Liu Bei established his capital in Shu and styled his state Han.
This marked forty-three years under two rulers.
He returned to serve under Emperor Yuan of the Wei dynasty.
In the first year of the Tai’an era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin, the *renxu* year,
Zhang Gui rose in Liangzhou and styled himself the ruler of Liang.
This was Former Liang.
It had seven rulers for sixty-two years before being absorbed into Former Qin under Fu Yonggu.
In the first year of the Yong’an era of Emperor Hui of Jin, the Jiazi year,
Liu Yuan rose in Pingyang;
he initially styled himself the successor to the Han and later called his state Zhao.
This was the Former Zhao dynasty.
It had four rulers and lasted for twenty-six years before being incorporated into the Later Zhao of Shi Le.
In the same year, the first year of Yong’an,
Li Xiong rose up in Shu;
he initially styled his reign the "Great Achievement" (Dàchéng).
Later, it was renamed Han.
It lasted for four rulers over forty-four years before being conquered by the Jin dynasty under Emperor Mu.
In the third year of the Taixing era of Emperor Yuan of the Eastern Jin, the Gengchen year,
Shi Le first established his capital at Xiangguo;
later, he moved the capital to Ye and styled his state Zhao.
This was the Later Zhao dynasty.
Including the thirty-five years of Ran Min,
it comprised four rulers before being absorbed by Former Yan under慕容俊 (Murong Jun).
In the eleventh year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Jin dynasty,
the year of Yimao (455 CE),慕容俊 (Murong Jun) founded Huanglong.
Later, he moved the capital to Ye and styled his state Yan.
This was Former Yan.
It lasted for nineteen years under two rulers before being annexed by Fu Yonggu of Former Qin.
In the *bingxu* year, the eleventh year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty,慕容垂 (Murong Chui) rose in Zhongshan and returned to assume the title of Yan;
this was known as Later Yan.
The capital was moved to Huanglong.
Five rulers reigned for twenty-six years before it fell to Feng Ba of Northern Yan.
In the twelfth year, the Dinghai year,
Lü Guang rose in Liangzhou and restored the state's title as Liang.
This is called Later Liang.
It had four rulers for sixteen years before being absorbed into Later Qin under Yao Xing.
In the first year of the Long’an era of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty,
the year Dingyou, Tufan Wuhuan rose in Xiping,
also styling himself as Liang.
This is called Southern Liang.
It had three rulers for eighteen years before it was annexed by the Western Qin under Qifu Chipan.
In the second year, the Wuxu year, Murong De rose at Guanggu;
he also styled himself Yan,
which was known as Southern Yan.
The two rulers [reigned] for thirteen years.
They were subsequently destroyed by the Jin Emperor An.
This reached the fourth year, the Gengzi year.
Li Tao rose in Dunhuang;
he was also titled Liang,
which is known as Xiliang (Western Liang).
The second ruler reigned for twenty-two years.
[He] entered the Northern Liang under Juqu Mengxun.
This was the third year of the Yixi era of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the Dingwei year.
Helian Bobo rose from the northern deserts;
he established his capital at the city of Tongwan and styled his state the Great Xia.
The three rulers reigned for twenty-five years.
This was from the entry [of the Later Yan] into Northern Wei during the reign of Emperor Taowu until the sixth year, the Gengxu year.
During this time, Feng Ba rose up and extinguished Later Yan.
The capital was at Changli;
it was styled Da Yan (Great Yan), which is known as Bei Yan (Northern Yan).
It had two rulers for twenty-eight years.
He also entered the court of Emperor Taiwu of the Northern Wei.
This was the year of Yimao, the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty,
which corresponds to the fifth year of the Taiyan era of the Northern Wei.
Emperor Taiwu’s western expedition subsequently led to the destruction of Northern Liang.
From that time on, various states were devoured by one another until they were nearly extinct;
only Northern Wei remained.
It reached the first year of the Longchang era of Emperor Ming of the Qi dynasty,
the Jiashu year; this was the eighteenth year of the Taihe era of Northern Wei,
when Emperor Xiaowen moved south to establish his capital at Luoyang.
In the sixth year of the Zhongdatong era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, which was the Jia-yin year,
corresponding to the third year of the Yongxi era of the Southern Wei,
Emperor Wu Yuanxun moved westward to Chang’an.
Following the precedent of Zhou Taizu Yuwen Helai,
Qi Taizu Gao Huang separately established Prince Yuan Shanjian of Qinghe as the sovereign,
with the northern capital at Ye.
Consequently, it was again divided into the Western and Eastern [dynasties].
In the fourth year of Chengsheng (the year of Yihai), the fourth year of the Chengsheng era of Emperor Xiaoyuan of the Liang dynasty, named Yi,
the capital was located at Jiangling.
It was extinguished by the Western Wei.
From this point on, the mandate of the Southern Dynasty turned northward.
That year was precisely the second year of the Later Yuan era of the Wei.
Xiao Yan’s grandson, Xia, was granted the succession by the Wei dynasty to continue the foundation of the Liang;
this is called the Later Liang.
Since it was a vassal state, it was merely a shadow kingdom.
The Zhou dynasty received the abdication of the Wei and consequently established itself there,
still maintaining its capital at Jiangling.
Three rulers presided over it for thirty-three years.
It ceased in the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, the Dingwei year.
It began when Emperor Wen of Wei received the abdication from the Later Han in the first year of the Huangchu era, the Gengzi year;
by the second year, the Xinchou year, the empire was divided into three parts.
In the fifty-ninth year,
the fifth year of the Xian-ning era of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, the year of Jihai,
the civil and military systems throughout the universe were once again unified.
From the twenty-third year [of the Jin dynasty] to the first year of Emperor Hui’s Yongning era, the year of Xinyou,
the territories of the various states were divided and vied with one another to establish their capitals;
this continued until the ninth year of the Kaihuang era, the year of Jiyou.
During the interval of two hundred and eighty-eight years,
the path of Heaven was indeed perilous even before the time of Shishen;
yet it remained as if the two hexagrams were in union.
Since the rise of the Great Liang, the Way of the King has been pure and tranquil.
The Nine Provinces have returned to their original state,
and nine years have passed since the unification of chariots and scripts.
The Wei dynasty, which transformed the world and benefited the people, cannot be fully extolled.
It lasted for forty-four reigns,
spanning three hundred and seventy-eight years, until the rise of the Great Sui.

The śramaṇa Zhu Falan from the kingdom of Central India was from his youth endowed with keen intelligence and refined elegance; he possessed broad learning and great versatility.

The various sūtra sections are extremely voluminous;

As these texts intermingle and overlap, it is truly difficult to authenticate and determine them.
There are those who have not seen the actual scriptures and merely peruse their titles;
there are those for whom there is an entry but no source, and those for whom there is neither entry nor translation.
Examining their origins, it is not that they lack a basis, but as the years have long passed, they are appended here at the end.
I hope that in the future, those of broad learning may encounter the original source;
I wish to retrieve the correct [teachings] to serve as a reliable standard,
clarifying the ocean of the Dharma so that its waves may be stilled.

Translations of the Sūtras during the Later Han (2) [and] the Wei and Wu Dynasties. *Chronicle of the Three Jewels through the Successive Dynasties*, Volume Five: Translations of the Sūtras during the Wei and Wu Dynasties.
Submitted by Your Subject Fei Changfang, Academician for the Translation of Sūtras.
Regarding the *Wei wu lu* (Records of Wei and Wu): these are the two imperial capitals of Luoyang and Jianye.
Cao Pi, whose courtesy name was Zihuan, was a native of Qiao in Pei Commandery and the eldest son of the Han Prime Minister Cao Cao.
On the day of his birth, there was a blue cloud shaped like a carriage canopy that remained emerald-green above him throughout the entire day.
Those who divined the vapors of the atmosphere declared:
The signs of supreme nobility are not those of a mere minister.
At the age of eight, he was skilled in composing literary works.
He succeeded to the相位 (xiàngwèi—Ministerial Position) as the Prince of Wei.
He succeeded to the Later Han and changed the name of the state to Wei,
continuing to have its capital at Luoyang.
The mandate of the flaming Han dynasty had reached its end;
the Five Peaks were to receive their sacrifices as two separate entities.
In the Huangchu era, Wei received the abdication of the throne.
Thereupon, the Nine Provinces were divided into three parts.
The Sun family established Wu,
relying on the Long River to plot for the empire.
Liu Zong ruled over Shu;
relying on the Jiegate Pass, he sought to stabilize the Central Plains.
Therein lay the tiger’s claws and fangs, and the dragon’s awesome power.
Each occupying its own domain, they were intent on devouring one another;
vying with one another to garrison their borders, they mutually maintained strict watchtowers and sentries.
They widely sought out men of talent and virtue to serve as their pillars and limbs.
The state honors the worthy and talented as its treasures;
now that such a master craftsman and sublime Dharma have arrived here together,
Senghui has accordingly come to Wu.
Śāriputra manifested his spiritual brilliance in the region south of the Yangtze River;
Kālaya traveled to the Wei state,
where the prohibitions and precepts were proclaimed throughout Luoyang.
The Dharma has thus spread extensively.
This is why, beginning with the Jianchu era, translators were specially established to adapt to the times;
they rendered the scriptures using local dialects according to the needs of each period.
Consequently, titles were assigned, resulting in the *Wu pin* (Pañcavimśati-sāhasrikā) and the *Shu pu yao* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).
As these were translated again and again in overlapping layers, it was from this that various lineages first branched out;
it is for this reason that the loss of the original translations lies precisely here.
Now that the three kingdoms of Wei, Shu, and Wu stand like tripod legs in mutual support,
why is it that only Shu lacks a dynastic record? Is this not because,
though the sun of the Buddha shines across the heavens, there were none with the karmic affinity [to receive its light]?
One cannot fail to observe that the thunder of the Dharma shakes the earth, yet those living in neighboring houses do not hear it.
Furthermore, although the old catalogs record that scriptures such as the *Shu Puyao* and the *Shou Lengyan* were translated in Shu,
they remain deficient regarding the translators' names, dates, and eras.
Should one wish to record and describe [these matters], one knows not where to rely;
as they fall into error when pushed back to their source,
there is no separate record.
Sun Quan, courtesy name Zhongmou,
was a native of Fuchun in Wu Commandery.
His family had served the state of Wu for generations.
On the eastern burial mound of his family home, divine light and vaporous clouds frequently appeared.
Furthermore, when Quan was first in her mother’s womb,
his mother dreamed that her intestines extended outward and encircled the gate of Wuchang.
The multitude all proclaimed, "The House of Sun shall flourish!
When Quan was born, his eyes possessed a supernatural radiance, his jaw was square, and his mouth was large;
his father marveled at these signs.
The Prince of Wǔ was a sovereign who spanned the capitals of Min and Yue, reaching as far as the constellations Dou and Niú;
he enfeoffed various lords and established an era name.
Having received the tribute of the seas and mountains and facing south to rule as sovereign, he styled his state Wu.
He moved the capital to Moling and changed its name to Jianye.
Wei succeeded Han, and two years later, Sun Quan established his reign.
The four rulers [of Wu] held power for fifty-nine years.
Two years after Sun Hao ascended the throne, the Wei dynasty abdicated to the Jin.
Fifteen years after the Jin was established, it pacified the region of Wu.
If categorized by year, the fourteenth year of [Sun] Hao’s reign should belong to the Jin dynasty;
however, we have now included it here in its entirety to compile it into the *Wu Lu* (Records of Wu).
This begins from the first year of the Huangchu era of Emperor Wen, the Gengzi year.
Reaching the first year of the Xianxi era of Emperor Yuan (Jia-shen),
there were five rulers and forty-five years in the interval;
ten individuals, both monastics and laypeople [were involved].
The sūtras, vinayas, and karmavācanas produced [in this period], together with those previously translated by unknown translators,
total three hundred and twelve works comprising four hundred and eighty-three fascicles.
These are compiled collectively as the *Shilu* (Record of the World) for the nine sovereigns and two capitals of the Wei and Wu dynasties.
[Furthermore, there is] the *Śīla* (Precepts) in one fascicle by the Wei śramaṇa Dharmakāla.
The two sections of four fascicles of sutras translated by the śramaṇa Saṃghavarman and the śramaṇa Tandi.

One hundred and ten sections, two hundred and ninety-one fascicles of sutras. 1. Wei Dynasty. 1. Dharmakāla’s *Mahāsāṃghika-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle. First appearance in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei-shi-lu*. The aforementioned one-fascicle *Prātimokṣa* was translated by the śramaṇa Dharmakāla from the country of Central India.
Wei Yunfashi was brilliant and gifted from childhood,
and his physical appearance was magnificent.
When he read a book, he could fully comprehend its literary meaning upon a single reading.

He was well-versed in the four Vedas, as well as the treatises on wind, clouds, stars, and the moon, and in diagrams and prophecies concerning the cycles of change; there was nothing he did not encompass.
He considered himself to have reached the ultimate limit of all worldly knowledge within the scope of his mind and eyes.
At the age of twenty-five, he entered a monastic dwelling.
I encountered the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* by Dharmottara;
I took it up briefly to examine it,
but I was utterly bewildered and could not understand it.
As he reflected with earnest diligence, his confusion and bewilderment increased all the more.
He then sighed, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma probes the profound and fully expounds the three periods of time."
He then abandoned his secular life to become a monk.
He recited the sutras of both the Mahayana and Hinayana as well as the various Vinaya collections,
and traveled to Luoyang to propagate the teachings.
At that time, although the Buddha-dharma existed within the borders of the Wei, the spirit of the Way was corrupted and declining.
There were also monks who had not yet received the precepts of refuge;
they merely distinguished themselves from the common people by shaving their hair.
Furthermore, although their fasting and repentance rituals were similar to those of sacrificial offerings,
once Kālaya arrived and extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma,
the monks requested him to bring forth the Vinaya.

Because the Kāśyapa [Vinaya] was composed according to the restrictive regulations of the Vinaya-piṭaka, its wording was verbose and extensive; as Buddhism had not yet flourished, it was certainly not accepted for use.
During the Jiaping era, he produced this one-fascicle *Śīlaskandha-sūtra* (Precept Manual) at Baima Monastery.
Furthermore, provisions were prepared for morning and evening meals;
the summer retreat (varṣā) regulations began from this point.
2. *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*, translated for the second time in two fascicles by Kang Seng Kai.
The first is titled *Yugalarāja-paripṛcchā-bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra*. It is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei-lu* (Wei Dynasty Catalogue).

There is also the two-fascicle *Amitāyus-sūtra*, a second translation, recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin-shi-za-lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and Baochang’s catalogue; it differs slightly from the version attributed to Lokakṣema. These two works comprise four fascicles in total.
The Indian śramaṇa Kang Sengkai translated [these texts] at the Baima Monastery in Luoyang during the Jiaping era of Emperor Qi’s reign.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* records them directly as the four sūtras beginning with the *Ugra-paripṛcchā*.

I have examined the *Dàozǔ Wèijìn lù* (Record of Daoist Ancestors of the Wei and Jin Dynasties), Sengyou’s *Chū sānzàng jì* (Record of the Translation of the Tripitaka), and Bǎochàng’s *Liángdài lù* (Record of the Liang Dynasty), among others.
The listings therein are as previously stated.
Beyond these, two other sections are not clearly identified; despite collating various records, they have not been found.
3. *Dharmatrāta-Dharmaguptaka-Karman*, one fascicle. First appeared in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei Lu*. Regarding the one fascicle titled *Dharmaguptaka*:
"Dharmaguptaka" is translated in Wei as "Dharma-Treasury."
The Tibetan master Dri ta yu was the ninth-generation disciple of A-yu-sha;
the Tibetan master succeeded him.
He was the founder of the Dharmaguptaka school.
From him, these various sub-sects arose;
this occurred during the second century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Later, the śramaṇa Tandi from the country of Anxi arrived at Luochui in the first year of the Gao-gui-xiang Gong era; being profoundly skilled in the Vinaya, he was requested by the assembly at Baima Temple to translate [the text].

4. *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* translated by Bo Yan, two fascicles; second appearance. Its text is largely identical to the version produced during the Han dynasty by Zhi Chen, with only minor differences.

This is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin Shi Za Lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and the *San Zang Ji* (Records of the Tripitaka). 5. *Wuliangqingjingpingdengjue-jing* (Sūtra of the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment), two fascicles; third appearance. Its text is largely identical to the versions of the *Wuliangshou-jing* (Sūtra of Immeasurable Life) produced by An Shigao, Kang Sengkai, and others, though the titles differ slightly. This is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin Shi Za Lu*. 6. *Chashu Lai Jing* (Sūtra of Kṣāranadi), one fascicle. One manuscript lacks the character "Cha" (Kṣāra).

The *Jichuzhen jing* (Sutra on the Elimination of Calamities), one fascicle, is seen in the catalogues of Zhu Daozu and Sengyou; the *Pingdengjue jing* (Sutra of Equal Enlightenment), one fascicle, is seen in the *Sanzang ji ji*; the *Pusa xiuxing jing* (Sutra on the Practice of the Bodhisattva), one fascicle—also known as the *Zhangzhe weishi suo wen pusa xiuxing jing* (Sutra on the Practice of the Bodhisattva Asked by the Elder Weishi)—is seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei wu lu*.
One work is titled *The Scripture on the Practice of a Householder*. It is found in the two catalogs compiled by Shi Xing and Baochang. The above six works comprise eight fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Gaogui of the Wei dynasty, the Western Region śramaṇa Bai Yan traveled to China to propagate the Way.
During the Gānlù era, he arrived in Luoyang and stayed at Baima Monastery.
The assembly requested him to translate [the scriptures].
5. Zhīqiángliáng translated the *Fǎhuá sānmèi jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi Sūtra) in six fascicles; one version contains the character "zhèng" (correct).
Yù states that the translator is lost. This one work in six fascicles was [translated] during the reign of Gāoguīxiānggōng,
in the seventh month of the first year of the Gānlù era, by the foreign śramaṇa Zhīqiángliángjiē.
Translated at Jiaozhou by Wei Yan Zheng Wuwe (the Correctly Fearless).
The śramaṇa Daosheng acted as the scribe.
Sengyou states that the translator is lost.
Sengfang examined and found it in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei-shi lu* (Record of the Wei Dynasty) and the *Shixing lu* (Record of Shixing).

If one were to follow the *Jiaozhou lu* (Record of Jiaozhou) and the *Shixing lu*, this work should have been included in the *Wu lu* (Record of Wu); however, it is now classified here based on its date and its inclusion in the *Wei lu*.
Attached hereto: 6.

*An-fa-xian-luo-mo-jia-jing* (The Scripture on the Arhat An-fa-xian), three fascicles; seen in the four catalogs of Zhu Daozu, Baochang, Fa-shang, and Lingyou. *Da-ban-nie-pan-jing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra), two fascicles; an abridgment of the first several chapters of the larger version, comprising these two fascicles.
According to the *Weilü* (Records of Wei) by Zhu Daozu, the first two sections together comprise five fascicles.
They were translated by the foreign śramaṇa An Faxian.
All bibliographical catalogs state this.
The Wei period does not distinguish which emperor’s reign year it belongs to;
for now, it is appended at the end according to the compilation.
Furthermore, it is also recorded in the *Bielu* (Separate Record).

2. Wu (Wu Dynasty), No. 1: *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Vighna-Akṣayamati*, four fascicles; recorded in the *Separate Record of the Wu Dynasty* (*Wu bie lu*). First appeared as the *Dharmapada-sūtra* in two fascicles; the original record of the Wu Dynasty states it was five fascicles; recorded in the *Records of the Tripitaka* (*San zang ji*). The above two works comprise six fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty, there was the Indian śramaṇa Vighna (in the Wu language,
meaning "obstruction"),
who was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and highly proficient in the four Āgamas.
He traveled through various kingdoms and regions, making the propagation of the Dharma his primary vocation.
Setting out from the Western Regions, he arrived at Jiangzuo accompanied by Zhu Luyan.
In the third year of the Huangwu era, he translated [the text] into the Wu script at Wuchang Commandery.
However, because Vighnanandi was not yet proficient in the local dialects,
there were some omissions during the translation from Sanskrit;
his intent lay in the fundamental meaning, and his phrasing was plain and unadorned.
2. *Dharmaratna-samāja-sūtra* (Zhū Lúyán Sānmójié jīng), one fascicle; recorded in the Shìxīng lù.
It is largely identical with minor differences to the *Vaṃśa-rāja-sūtra*.

*Brahmacarya-sūtra* (Fànzhì jīng), one fascicle; recorded in the Shìxīng lù; the same root text as the *Pañca-brāhmaṇa-śata-sūtra*, but a different translation. *Buddha-vaidya-sūtra* (Fóyī jīng), one fascicle; translated jointly by Zhīyuè.
These are not complete texts; they are seen in brief according to the *Bǎochàng lù*.
It is said that these three scriptures, including the *Fó yīwáng jīng*, together comprise three fascicles.
They were [translated] during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty.
The Indian śramaṇa Zhu Lüyán translated [the text] for Sun Quan at the capital of Yang after the death of Weiqinan.
The various catalogs differ:
some say *Jiangyan*, some say *Chiyen*,
and others say *Lüyan*.
It is not clear which of these is correct;
therefore, I have listed them all for reference. 3.
Zhi Qian’s *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dà míngdù jīng) in four fascicles is also called the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-ananta Sūtra* (Dà míngdù wújí jīng), or it is in six fascicles.

I have seen the *Zhu Daozu Wei Wu deng san lu* (The Three Catalogues of Zhu Daozu of the Wei and Wu Dynasties), which records the *Chan miyao jing* (Sūtra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna) in four fascicles, also known as the *Chanfa miyao* (Secret Essentials of the Dhyāna Method); I have also seen the *Wu bie er lu* (Two Separate Catalogues of the Wu Dynasty), which records the *Achamo pusa jing* (Akṣayamati-bodhisattva Sūtra) in four fascicles.
Second appearance.
This differs slightly from the original text translated previously by Vighna.

The *Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhānasaṃgraha-sūtra* in four fascicles is said to have been compiled by the Indian śramaṇa Saṃghasena; it is also transmitted as being in three fascicles. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-acintyadharmamukha-sūtra* in three fascicles is also called the *Buddhabhāṣita-sarvatrāmārgapraveśa-sūtra*.
Alternatively, it consists of two fascicles.
This second edition differs slightly from the one translated by Yan Fotiao of the Later Han dynasty.

I have seen the *Wei wu lu* (Record of Wei and Wu) by Zhu Daozu and the *San zang ji* (Records of the Tripitaka), which list a two-fascicle *Xiu xing fang bian jing* (Sūtra on the Expedient Means of Practice)—some versions of which include the character "chan" (dhyāna)—as well as a two-fascicle *Mo he ban nie pan jing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra) recorded in the *Wu lu*. This latter version abridges the introductory section and the "Chapter on Lamentation" of the large edition into two fascicles.
The final three scrolls differ slightly [from the others].
According to Zhu Daozu’s *Wu lu*, Dao’an stated that it was excerpted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Sengyou states:

"The present *Dīrgha Āgama* differs from this [version]. This second translation, the *Ruiying benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Auspicious Responses and Origins) in two fascicles, was produced during the Huangwu era.
It is also called the *Taizi benqi ruiying* (Auspicious Responses to the Prince’s Origins)."
This differs slightly from the version translated by Kang Mengxiang.
It was transcribed by Xie Qiang of Chenjun and Zhang Xi of Wujun, among others.
Wei Dong’ewang Zhi verified and finalized it. This is recorded in the Shixing lu and the Sanzang ji; the two-fascicle *Fajing jing* is not listed in Dao’an’s catalog.
Sengyou states that he saw it in the *Bielu* (Separate Record).

Senghui’s commentary and preface to the two-fascicle *Xiao achamujing* (Smaller Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra) are seen in the *Bielu* and the *Sanzang ji*. The two-fascicle *Amiduojing* (Amitābha-sūtra), the fourth edition, is also recorded therein.
It differs slightly from the versions translated by An Shigao of the Han dynasty and Seng Kai of the Wei dynasty.

Its internal title reads *The Scripture on Amitābha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyak-saṃbuddha, Who Transfers Human Beings*, also known as the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*. It is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Wu lu* (Record of Wu) as the *Yizu jing* (Scripture of Meaningful Feet) in two fascicles. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in two fascicles was the second edition produced during the Huangwu era.
It differs slightly from the version translated by Zhi Chen during the Later Han dynasty.
It is not found in the *Wu lu* or the *An lu* compiled by Zhu Daozu. Sengyou states that he saw it in the *Bie lu*.

The *Faju jing* (Dharmapada-sūtra) in two fascicles is the second translation; it is seen in the *Bie lu* and the *Sanzang ji*, and is slightly superior to the previous translation. The *Huiyin jing* (Prajñā-mudrā-sūtra), also known as the *Huiyin sanmei jing*, consists of one fascicle.
One version is titled *The Scripture on All Buddhas of the Ten Directions Standing Firmly Before One*;
another is titled *The Scripture on the Wisdom Seal Samādhi of the Precious Field*.
These two are different translations of the same original text as the *Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā-sūtra*.

I have seen one fascicle of the *Bunyōkyō* (Sutra on the Original Vows), also titled the *Bosatsu Hongyōkyō* (Sutra on the Original Vows of the Bodhisattva), in the *Wulu* by Zhu Daozu and in the *Sanzangji*. It is recorded in the *Yulu* [of Sengyou]. There is also one fascicle of the *Surai-kyō* (Sutra of Surata); this second edition is the same text as that translated by Bo Yan, though it is a separate recension.
One version is titled the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Sulāta*.

It is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Wulu* and the *Sanzang ji*. There is one fascicle of the *Fanmayu jing*, recorded in Zhu Daozu’s catalog and the *Sanzang ji*. There is also one fascicle of the *Si'amo jing*; Zhu Da'an states that "Si'amo" is another name for [Sulāta].

This is the *Bodhisattvamārgavṛkṣasūtra*, a different translation from the same original source with a distinct title. According to the three catalogs by Dao’an, Zhi Min-du, and Sengyou, it is also known as the *Weimi chi jing* (one fascicle), or alternatively, the *Wuliangmen weimi chi jing*.
I have seen the *Sengrui erqin lu* and the *Sanzang ji*: the *Yueming tongzi jing* (one fascicle), also called the *Yueming tongnan jing* or the *Yueming pusa sanmei jing*;
I have seen the *Anan sishi jing* (one fascicle) in the *Sanzang ji* and the *Bie lu*; and the *Chamojie jing* (one fascicle), also known as the *Pusa shengdi jing*.

Zhu Daozu’s *Wulu* records one fascicle of the *Uttaramātṛ-sūtra* (one version lacks the character "mātṛ"); one fascicle of the *Saptakanyā-sūtra*, which An Shigao states was extracted from the *Abhidharma* (one source calls it the *Nüben jing*);
and first, one fascicle of the *Ugra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, with a second [fascicle] subsequently produced.

The *Wu lu* (Records of Wu) by Zhu Daozu lists either one or two fascicles; the *Bashi jing* (Sūtra of the Eight Teachers), one fascicle; and the *Shi monan benjing* (Original Sūtra of Śramaṇa Maṇava), one fascicle, which appears in the *Madhyama Āgama*.
According to the *Wulu* (Records of Wu) by Zhu Daozu, one fascicle of the *Bochao jing* (Excerpted Scripture on the Parable of the Wise Man) first appeared;
this is the same as the *Bo jing*.
According to the *Sanzang ji* (Record of the Tripitaka) and the *Bielu* (Separate Record), one fascicle of the *Lao nüren jing* (Sutra of the Old Woman) was translated from the Abhidharma.
The *Wulu* states directly that it is either the *Lao nü jing* (Sūtra of the Old Woman) or the *Lǎo mǔ jīng* (Sūtra of the Old Mother).
It is seen in the *Sanzang ji* as the first appearance of one fascicle of the *Zhai jing* (Fasting Sūtra);
another version calls it the *Chizhai jing* (Sūtra on Observing the Fast).

In the *Bié lù huìguò fǎ jīng* (Sutra on the Method of Repentance from a Separate Record), one fascicle—also titled *Xù shífāng lǐbài huìguò wén* (Preface to the Text for Prostrations and Repentance to the Ten Directions)—it is stated:

"The *Xiánzhě dé jīng* (Sutra on the Virtues of the Worthy One), one fascicle; the *Fó cóng shàng suǒ xíng sānshí shǐ jīng* (Sutra on the Thirty Verses on the Buddha’s Conduct Above), one fascicle—or without the word 'sutra' [in the title]; and the *Liǎoběn shēngsǐ jīng* (Sutra on the Fundamental Understanding of Birth and Death), one fascicle. Thus says Dao'an.
Regarding the *Chusheng jing* (Sūtra on Birth):
Sengyou states that it currently consists of five fascicles;
however, this title does not appear in the *Sheng jing* (Sūtra on Birth).
One title is *Dàgān Tóngběn Yìchū* (The Rice Stalks: Same Root, Different Origins).

Xuanzang himself annotated it and composed a preface; it consists of only twenty verses and one fascicle, or perhaps lacks the word "sūtra" [in the title]. There is also the *Nǚlóngshī Jīng* (Sūtra of the Dragon-Giving Woman), one fascicle, which is not included in Dao'an’s catalog.
Sengyou states that he saw one fascicle of the *Mṛgāraputra-sūtra* in the *Bie lu*; it is not in Seng’an’s catalogue.

Sengyou states that he saw it in the *Bie lu* as well as in Zhu Daozu’s *Wu lu*, where it is also recorded; there is also one fascicle of the *Dafangdeng shiermen jing*, which is not in Seng’an’s catalogue.
Sengyou states that the *Laita-heluo jing* (Rāṣṭrapāla-sūtra) in one fascicle is found in the *Bielu* (Separate Record), being the second appearance [of this text].
It differs slightly from the version translated by Zhi Yao.
Some also call it the *Luohan Laita-heluo jing* (The Arhat Rāṣṭrapāla Sūtra).
An’s record does not exist;
Yu states that he saw it in a separate record.
It consists of thirty scriptures in forty-eight fascicles.
Excluding the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*,
all [other versions] are found in Sengyou’s Catalogue as the one-fascicle *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*, the second translation,
which differs slightly from that translated by Kāśyapa Mātanga.
The literary meaning is correct and the phrasing is worthy of admiration. See the *Bie lu* (Separate Record):

the *Nan Longwang jing* (Sutra of the Dragon King Nan) in one fascicle—one manuscript lacks the character "Wang" (King)—and the *Bu zishouyi jing* (Sutra on Not Guarding One's Own Mind) in one fascicle, also called the *Zishou* (Self-Guarding).

*Or-yun pu-tzu shou wu-yin shih ching* (Sūtra on Not Guarding the Five Aggregates), one fascicle; *Ch'i-chih ching* (Sūtra of the Seven Knowledges), one fascicle—also titled *Chih*; from the first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama*; *Min-jen ch'iu-yüan ching* (Sūtra on People Seeking Their Wishes), one fascicle; *Fo k'ai-chieh a-p'o fan-chih ching* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Explanation for the Brahmin A-ba), one fascicle—also said to be the *Fan-chih a-p'o ching*; from the *Dīrgha Āgama*; *Pao-hai fan-chih ch'eng-chiu ta-pei ching* (Sūtra on the Brahmin Pao-hai Accomplishing Great Compassion), one fascicle; *Fan-chih tzu ssŭ tao p'ai ching* (Sūtra on the Death of the Brahmin’s Son and the Failure of the Rice), one fascicle; *Fan-chih wên fo shih ching* (Sūtra on the Brahmin Asking the Buddha about His Teacher), one fascicle; *Kiang ch'ien fan-chih ching* (Sūtra on Subduing a Thousand Brahmins), one fascicle;

from the *Āgama*; *Fan-chih ching* (Brahmin Sūtra), one fascicle; secondly, *Tu fan-chih ching* (Sūtra on Converting the Brahmin), one fascicle; *Wai-tao hsien-ni shuo tu ching* (Sūtra on the Heretic Śreṇika Explaining Emancipation), one fascicle.

*The Brahmaṇa’s Sūtra on the Purity of Bonds*, one fascicle; *The Brahmaṇa’s Questioning of the Buddha on the Increase and Decrease of the World*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Departure from Desire Spoken by the Buddha for the Non-Buddhist Susīma*, one fascicle (also titled *Susīma*); *The Brahmajāla Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views*, one fascicle—these are recorded in the *Separate Catalog*.

Sengyou states: *The Sūtra of King Aji* (one fascicle), translated by Dharmarakṣa; *The Sūtra of King Jietan*; *The Sūtra on the Five Dharmas Accomplished by a King for Long Endurance in the World* (one fascicle); *The Sūtra of the Simile of the Lion’s Milk of King Weilou* (one fascicle—some versions lack the word "simile"); *The Sūtra of the Root of All Dharmas* (one fascicle); *The Sūtra of the Five Mothers and Sons* (one fascicle); *The Sūtra on the Precepts that Subdue and Eliminate Calamities* (one fascicle); *The Sūtra of the Withered Tree* (one fascicle, found in the old catalogues; found in Dao’an’s catalogues, with large characters at the beginning); *The Sūtra of What is Mine* (one fascicle); *The Sūtra of the Path of Ambrosia from the Birth [of the Buddha]* (one fascicle—found in the *Chuyao jing*); *The Sūtra on the Contemplation of Impurity* (one fascicle—found in the *Dīrgha Āgama*); *The Sūtra of the Bubble on Water* (one fascicle); *The Sūtra of the Precepts on the Ganges River* (one fascicle—found in the old catalogues).

*The Sūtra on the Impermanence of Form Without the Word "Precepts"* (1 fascicle); from the Āgama. *The Sūtra on Guarding Speech and Mind* (1 fascicle); *The Sūtra on the Shortness of Life* (1 fascicle); from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. *The Sūtra on the Superiority of Dharma-Giving* (1 fascicle); *The Sūtra on the Exhaustion of All Outflows* (1 fascicle); from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Alternatively, it is said that there is a single fascicle titled *Zhujing xingxiu cijing* (Compassion Sutra on the Practice of All Exhaustions).

*The Sūtra of the Elder Sumati*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of King Māndhātṛ*, one fascicle. Originally issued as one version, it lacked the character "King" (王). *The Sūtra of the Four Vows*, one fascicle. Seen in the *Wu lu* (Record of Wu) by Zhu Daozu and the *San zang ji* (Records of the Tripitaka). *The Sūtra on the Chapter of Pure Conduct*, one fascicle. Issued from the *Avataṃsaka*; also called the *Sūtra on the Original Acts of the Bodhisattva*. *The Sūtra of the Vajra Purity*, one fascicle. Also called the *Sūtra of the Vajrasamādhi of Innate Purity, Neither Extinct Nor Destroyed*. *The Sūtra of Various Difficulties of Weiyue*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Buddha Preaching the Dharma for the Hārītī Ghost of the Wilderness*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Aśokadattā, Daughter of King Ajātaśatru*, one fascicle. Originally issued as the *Sūtra Encouraging the Study of the Way*, one fascicle. One version lacks the character "Encourage" (勸). *The Sūtra of Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Palm-leaf Tree*, one fascicle. Secondly issued as the *Sūtra of Resolute Mind* (*Kṣānti-mati*), one fascicle; sometimes written with the character "Mind" (心).

*The Scripture on the Three Grades of Disciples*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on Great Diligence*, one fascicle (also called *The Scripture on Great Diligence*); *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Practice*, one fascicle (listed in Baochang’s record); *The Scripture of the Bodhisattva Puguang*, one fascicle (listed in a separate record); *The Scripture of the Dharani-Phrase Spell*, one fascicle (also called *The Scripture of the Upholding Phrase Spell*); *The Scripture of the Flower-Accumulation Dharani Spell*, one fascicle (listed in Baochang’s record); *The Scripture of the Eight Auspicious Ones*, one fascicle (listed in ancient records; it also contains the word "spell").

*Chūchū maha-banruo boluomi zhòujīng* (The Sutra on the Spell of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā) in one fascicle; listed in the *Bǎochàng lù*, or simply called *Banruo boluomi zhòujīng*. *Qīfó shénzhòujīng* (The Sutra of the Divine Spells of the Seven Buddhas) in one fascicle; one version lacks the word "sutra" (*jīng*). *Dàcí wújiǎn jīng* (The Sutra of Great Compassion Without Diminution) in one fascicle. *Bǎonǚ míng sānshí'èr xiàng jīng* (The Sutra of the Precious Woman Clarifying the Thirty-two Marks); also known as the *Wèn huì jīng* (The Sutra of Inquiring about Wisdom).
Also known as the *Sūtra on the Thirty-two Matters* or the *Sūtra of the Questions of the Jewel Woman*;

it has four titles in total. The *Sūtra of the Three Fish Losing Water*, one fascicle; the *Sūtra Expounding the Deeds of the Secular and the Monastic*, one fascicle (found in the old catalogs, sometimes without the character "deeds"); the *Sūtra of the Adorned and Unadorned Woman*, one fascicle (found in the Baochang lu); the *Sūtra of Shenri*, one fascicle; and the *Sūtra of Sundarika*, one fascicle (from the Madhyama Āgama), also called the *Sūtra of the Brahmin Sundarika*. Dao'an stated [these were translated by him].

*Chūzhōng āhán zhǎngzhě yīnyuè jīng* (The Madhyama Āgama Sūtra on the Householder Yīnyuè), one scroll; also known as *Zhǎngzhě yīnyuè bùlánjiāshè jīng*. *Yījì zhū yīnyuè jīng hēishì fànlì jīng* (The Sūtra on Yīnyuè and the Brahmin Hēishì), one scroll;

listed in the *Bié lù*. *Fǎlǜ jīng* (The Sūtra on Dharma and Vinaya), one scroll; also known as *Fǎlǜ sānmèi jīng*. *Chūjiā gōngdé jīng* (The Sūtra on the Merit of Leaving Home), one scroll; listed in the *Wú lù*. *Bìmó shì mùlián jīng* (The Sūtra on Māra Tempting Maudgalyāyana), one scroll; listed in the *Jiù lù*. *Chū āpítán qī lòu jīng* (The Abhidharma Sūtra on the Seven Leaks), one scroll; listed in the *Bié lù*. *Lándá wáng jīng* (The Sūtra of King Lándá), one scroll; also known as *Mùlián yīnyuán gōngdé jīng*.
Some call it the *Maudgalyāyana-guṇa-sūtra*.

In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, the Imperial Scribe for Translating Scriptures, Your Subject Fei Changfang, presents the Record of the Western Jin:
Sima Yan, styled Anshi, was a native of Wen in Henei.
He was the crown prince of Prince Zhao of Jin, who served as the Grand General of Wei, Palace Attendant, Director of the Secretariat, and Chancellor.
When Emperor Zhao passed away, Emperor Yan succeeded him as king.
Realizing that the mandate of the calendar had shifted,
Emperor Yuan sent the Grand Guardian Zheng Chong to present the imperial seal and transfer the throne to him.
Yan received the abdication while sitting with his hands folded,
and thus became Emperor Wu.
He styled the Jin dynasty as having its capital in Luoyang and Chang’an.
These were the former capitals of the East and West.
During the fifteenth year of Emperor Wu of Jin’s reign,
in the Xianning era, he commanded Sima Zhou to pacify Wu, thereby capturing Sun Hao.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Return-to-the-Refuge (Guiming Hou).
From the twenty-fourth year of the Yong’an era of the Later Han until the beginning of the first year of the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty, the year of Gengzi,
the nine provinces were once again unified under a single rule.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty, Lu Ji said:
"From now until sixty years hence..."
Under Heaven, carriages shall have uniform ruts and scripts shall have uniform characters.
At this point, it was indeed just as Yuexi had said.
Sixty years were to pass before the subjugation of Shu and the destruction of Wu.
Twenty years later, at the beginning of Emperor Hui’s Yongning era,
the way of governance declined and collapsed while the various regional powers rose like mountain peaks.
Prince Zhao established a foundation for rebellion and usurped the throne within the court.
Zhang Gui followed in his predecessor’s footsteps yet failed to submit as a vassal, usurping control of the Liang territories;
with internal and external affairs in turmoil, the foundations of disorder gradually took root,
which is why Liu Yuan established himself at Pingyang.
Li Xiong thus took advantage of the celestial mandate;
Emperor Huai was reduced to wandering in the Xiang Valley,
and Emperor Min fled from Chang’an.
Since the Way relies on its times for its flourishing, yet both capitals were in a state of ruin;
and since the Dharma is manifested through its adherents,
it fell upon two rulers who were beset by turmoil and distress.
The myriad people were scattered and disunited, finding no one in whom they could place their trust;
the hundred officials lost their posts, and the Śākya lineage was left without refuge.
At that time, there were the śramaṇas Dharmarakṣa, Qiángliánglóuzhì, and others, who sacrificed themselves for the benefit of sentient beings and vowed to propagate the teachings widely.
He did not shrink from hardship or toil, making the propagation of the Dharma his primary mission.
During the Jin dynasty, he was the most prolific translator of scriptures.
His disciples included Dharmakṣema, Nie Chengyuan and his son, Zhu Falan, and others.
Successively, they transmitted and expounded [the teachings].
Thus, within fifty years, thirteen individuals—
both Chinese and foreign, monastic and lay— [attained realization].
Together with the previously lost translations of various sūtras, precepts,
and other texts, there are a total of four hundred and fifty-one works in seven hundred and seventeen fascicles.
This constitutes the record of fifty-two years under four emperors across the two capitals of the Western Jin dynasty.
