it is a separate translation of the same text as the *Shizhi jing* (Śrīmālā-sūtra). It is also included in the *Daji zongde sanmei jing* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Collection of All Virtues) in three fascicles, or as it is otherwise called.
The *Sarvapuṇyasamuccaya-samādhi-sūtra*, in either two fascicles;
listed in the record of Nie Daozhen. Also the *Sūryaprabhāsa-samādhi-sūtra* in three fascicles, translated in the first month of the seventh year of the Taishi era.
When it first appeared,
it was either in two fascicles or simply titled the *Chāorìmíng jīng* (Sūtra of Surpassing the Sun’s Radiance).

I saw the *Record of Nie Daozhen* containing the three fascicles of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, the three fascicles of the *Sarva-mantra-sūtra*, and the two fascicles of the *Ratnacūḍa-paripṛcchā-sūtra*; these were issued on the fourteenth day of the seventh month of the first year of the Taixi era.
The *Mahāsannipāta* is also known as the *Bodhisattva-viśuddha-caryā-sūtra*.

An old catalogue states that the *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra* is found in the record of Nie Daozhen; the *Sujāti-devaputra-sūtra* in two fascicles was translated at the Baima Monastery within the Qing Gate in Chang’an in the second year of the Taishi era.
An Wenhui, Bai Yuanshin, and Nian Chengyuan transmitted the oral instructions; Zhang Xuanbo and Sun Xiuda recorded them in writing.
It is also called the *Sūtra on the Four Questions*.
It appears in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* as the two-fascicle *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-sūtra*, translated in the first year of the Taixi era.
Some say "adorned and purified Buddha-fields," while others say "Buddha-fields adorned and purified.

See Zhu Daozu’s *Jin shi za lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and the two-fascicle *Hongdao guangxian sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Propagation of the Way), translated in the third month of the second year of the Yongjia era.
One says Anavatapta;
another says Anavatapta invited the Buddha; another says the Samādhi of the Vajra Gate.
Sometimes the word "samādhi" is omitted.
In total there are four versions comprising ten chapters:
one version contains only seven chapters, lacking the middle three; another version contains only the first five chapters.

According to the record of Nie Daozhen, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in two fascicles was translated on the third day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Taishi era; it is also called the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
According to the *Nie Daozhen lu*, the two-fascicle *Wuliangshou jing* was translated on the twenty-first day of the first month in the second year of the Yongjia era;
this is the fourth translation.

Its text is identical to the versions produced during the Wu period by Zhi Qian, and during the Wei period by Kang Sengkai and Bai Yan, though the titles differ; it is also called the *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing*.

In the *Jin Shi Za Lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) by Zhu Daozu, it is noted that there is a separate version of the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* in two fascicles; this distinct edition of the *Śūraṃgama* states that Ānanda spoke it. There is also the *Ratnagarbha-sūtra* in two fascicles, which appeared in the sixth year of the Taishi era. There is further the *Sāratama-saṃgraha-sūtra* in two fascicles, also known as the *Sarvabuddhasārasamuccaya-sūtra*. Regarding the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra* in two fascicles, Dao’an stated: [text follows].
Furthermore, there are two fascicles of the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra* (also known as the *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya Sūtra*), translated in the sixth month of the sixth year of the Taikang era.
Its initial publication was also titled the *Mahā-upāya-kauśalya Sūtra Asked by Bodhisattva Hui-shang*.
Some call it the *Huishang pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Prajñottara);
some, *Shanquan fangbian* (Expedient Skillful Means);
and others, *Fangbian suodu wuji* (The Immeasurable of Expedient Deliverance).

It has five names in total: it is recorded in the *Nie Daozhen Lu* as the *Shunquan Fangbian Jing* (Sutra on Following Expedient Means) in two fascicles; it is also called the *Zhuan Nüshen Pusa Jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva Transforming the Female Body);
and it is also called the *Tuiquan Fangbian Jing* (Sutra on Pushing Aside Expedient Means).
The *Jiulù* (Old Catalogue) states:
The *Suíquán nǚ jīng* (Sūtra of the Girl Suíquán) is found in the *Niè Dàozhēn lù*;

the *Suíquán nǚ jīng* in two fascicles is found in the *Biělù* (Separate Catalogue). The *Rúhuàn sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra of the Samādhi of Illusion-like Nature) in two or three fascicles is absent from the *Ānlù* (An’s Catalogue). The *Púsà jīng* (Bodhisattva Sūtra) in two or three fascicles and the *Yǒngfú dìng jīng* (Sūtra of the Heroic Subduing Samādhi) in two fascicles appeared on the ninth day of the fourth month of the first year of Yuánkāng.
This is the fourth translation.
It shares the same title as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* produced by Lokakṣema, Zhi Qian, Bai Yan, and others, though the wording differs slightly.

According to the *Nie Zhendao Lu*, there were further translations produced during the Taishi era: the two-fascicle *Ajātaśatru-rāja Sūtra*; the second production of the two-fascicle *Vaṇija Sūtra*; the two-fascicle *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnagarbha Sūtra*, also known as the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-pariśuddhi Sūtra*; and the two-fascicle *Buddhāvataraṇa-trāyastriṃśa-deva-loka-mātṛ-dharma-deśanā Sūtra*.
It is also called the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Ascent to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven*.

The *Record of Nie Daozhen* lists one fascicle of the *Renwang Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, or alternatively two fascicles, as seen in the miscellaneous records of the Jin dynasty. There is also one fascicle of the *Pumenpin Sūtra*, translated in the first month of the eighth year of Taikang.
In the *Jiè Dàozhēn Lù*, it is recorded that there is one fascicle of the *Yuèguāng Tóngzǐ Jīng* (Sūtra of the Youth Moonlight), also called the *Yuèmíng Tóngzǐ Jīng* (Sūtra of the Youth Moonbright).
It is grouped together with the three sūtras concerning Shēnrì, Dōushīlìyuè, and others.
*The Sūtra on the Practice of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; translated at the West Temple in Chang’an during the seventh year of the Yuankang era.

*The Sūtra of the Great Pure Dharma Gate*, one fascicle; issued from the twenty-second fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; issued on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Jianxing era.

According to the record compiled by Nie Daozhen, there is one fascicle of the *Li gou shi nü jing* (Sūtra on the Woman Free from Defilement through Giving), issued on the second day of the second month in the tenth year of the Taikang era.
Also according to the record compiled by Nie Daozhen, there is one fascicle of the *Xumoti pusa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Sumati), also known as the *Xumoti jing*.
It is also called the *Sūma Sūtra*.
According to the catalogs of Nie Daozhen, Zhu Daozu, and others, there is one fascicle of the *Longshi nü jing* (Sūtra of the Daughter of Longshi),
which older catalogs refer to as the *Longshi benqi jing* (Sūtra of the Original Arising of Longshi).
The second is the *Mahāvaipulya-uṣṇīṣarāja-sūtra*, one fascicle, first translated.
It is also called the *Uṣṇīṣarāja-sūtra*,
the *Vimalakīrti-putra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, and the *Sudharmacintin-kumāra-sūtra*.

There are four titles in total. According to Zhi Min-du’s *Catalogue*, there is the *Wusuoxiwang jing* (Sutra on Having No Expectations), one fascicle; it is also called the *Xiangbu jing* (Elephant-Step Sutra) and the *Xiangyi jing* (Elephant-Axilla Sutra).
According to Nie Daozhen’s *Catalogue*, there is the *Moni jing* (Sutra on the Māra Reversal), one fascicle, which appeared on the second day of the twelfth month of the tenth year of Taikang.
I have seen one fascicle of the *Ji zhū fāngděng xué jīng* (Record of the Salvation of Various Mahāyāna Students) by Niè Dàozhēn; sometimes the character "xué" (student) is omitted.

I have also seen one fascicle of the *Púsà xíng wǔshí yuánshēn jīng* (Sūtra on the Fifty Circumstances of the Bodhisattva’s Body) by Zhú Dàozǔ of the Jìn dynasty, also known as the *Wǔshí yuánshēn xíng jīng*.
It is also called the *Bodhisattva-yuan-shen-wushi-shi-jing* (Sūtra on the Fifty Matters Concerning the Bodhisattva’s Body).

According to Zhu Daozu’s *Jin-shi-za-lu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty), it is the one-fascicle *Mile-pusa-so-wen-benyuan-jing* (Sūtra on the Original Vows Asked by Maitreya Bodhisattva), translated on the seventeenth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Dà'ān era.
Also known as the *Sūtra on the Original Vows of Maitreya Bodhisattva* and the *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Questions*.
Recorded in the catalogues of Nie Daozhen and Zhu Daozu. One fascicle of the *Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-śīla-sūtra*, translated on the eighth day of the fourth month in the tenth year of the Taikang era.
While Hù was at Baima Monastery in Luoyang, he encountered the Western Region śramaṇa Jìzhì, who recited this sūtra for him.

Although several chapters remained that he had completely forgotten, he transmitted only those he could remember; Nè Dàozhēn acted as the scribe. This is recorded in Zhú Dàozǔ’s catalogue. One source calls it the *Jìnglǜ jīng* (Sūtra on Pure Discipline); another, the *Wúsīyì háotóng púsà jīng* (Sūtra of the Inconceivable Childlike Bodhisattva) in one fascicle; and yet another, the *Wúsīyì guāng suowèn jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions of Inconceivable Light).
Also known as the *Acintyaprabhāsa-sūtra* or the *Maitreya-buddhatva-sūtra*, one fascicle;

translated in the second year of the Tai’an era. Also titled the *Maitreya-āgami-janma-sūtra*, found in the *Nie Daozhen lu*. The *Śāriputra-Maudgalyāyana-caryā-deśa-sūtra*, one fascicle; also called the *Śāriputra-Mahāmaudgalyāyana-caryā-catuḥpatha-sūtra*. The *Vaidūryarāja-sūtra*, one fascicle. The *Ratnadattā-dārikā-sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled the *Sumati-dharma-vinaya-samādhi-sūtra*.

The *Jiè Dàozhēn Lù Fó Wéi Púsà Wǔ Mèng Jīng* (Record of Jiè Dàozhēn on the Five Dreams of the Buddha as a Bodhisattva), one fascicle, translated in the fifth month of the second year of the Tà'ān era.
It is also titled *Fó Wǔ Mèng* (The Five Dreams of the Buddha) and *Tàizǐ Wǔ Mèng* (The Five Dreams of the Crown Prince).

One title is *The Five Dreams of a Rishi*. It is found in the *Jiùlù* (Old Catalogue) and the *Niè Dàozhēn Lù* (Record of Niè Dàozhēn). *The Original Scripture of Mahāmaudgalyāyana*, one scroll; some versions lack the character "jiàn" (目). *The Scripture on the Tomb-Spirit of the Crown Prince*, one scroll. *The Second Translation of the Scripture on the Four Unobtainables*, one scroll; found in the records of Niè Dàozhēn and Zhèngdù et al. *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Method for Repenting Transgressions*, one scroll; sometimes the word "jīng" (scripture) is omitted.
The sub-note states:

"The *Lungshu Shizhu Lun* (Nāgārjuna’s *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*) contains the *Ruguang Jing* (Milk-Light Sūtra), one fascicle; the *Duzi Jing* (Gokulika Sūtra); the *Ben Tongyi Bie Xinming Nü Fanzhi Fu Fanzhi Shi Jing* (Sūtra on the Brahmin Woman Xinming Offering Rice Water, translated separately from the same original as the Gokulika Sūtra), one fascicle, also simply called the *Xinming Jing*; and the *Daliu Xiangbai Jing* (Sūtra of the Six Great Prostrations), one fascicle, translated in the first year of the Tai’an era."
Some call it the *Śikhālaputra-ṣaḍ-abhimukha-praṇāma-sūtra*;

others simply call it the *Ṣaḍ-abhimukha-praṇāma-sūtra*. According to the records of Zhi Mindu and Baochang, there is a one-fascicle *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra*, also known as the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* or the *Aṅgulimāra-sūtra*.
I have seen the *Record of Nie Daozhen* containing one fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmika-sūtra*, which is largely the same with minor differences as the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra*.
Also, one fascicle of the *Māndhātṛ-rāja-sūtra*, the second edition.
It is largely the same as, yet slightly different from, the version translated by Wu Shi Qian.

It consists of one fascicle of the *Six Pāramitās Collection: Illuminating Samādhi Sūtra* and one fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Desires that Cause Suffering*, both translated in the first month of the third year of the Taian era.
According to the records of Nie Daozhen, Wang Zong, and others, there is one fascicle titled *Famojin jing* (or alternatively written as *Miejing*),
also known as the *Kongji pusa suowen jing*.
The second translation is identical to that produced by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty, titled *Bodhisattva-cai-fa-jing* (one scroll), sometimes omitting the word "jing.
It is also known as *Zheng-zhai* (Right Fasting) or *Chi-zhai* (Maintaining Fasting).

*The Scripture on the Method for the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha’s Sole Realization of the Self-Vowed Samādhi*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture on the Tathāgata’s Self-Vowed Samādhi*. *The Scripture on the Past Buddhas’ Almsround*, one fascicle—also referred to as *The Scripture on Seeing the Five Hindrances and Doubtful Knots Causing the Loss of Practice* according to the old catalogues. Translated on the twelfth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Yongning era.

In the *Jiè Dàozhēn Lù*, there is recorded one fascicle of the *Zǒngchí Jīng* (Scripture on Total Retention) and the *Chūshēng Jīng* (Scripture on Birth). Some say it is the *Fóxīn Zǒngchí Jīng* (Scripture on the Buddha-Mind Total Retention);

there is also one fascicle of the *Wǔfú Shījīng* (Scripture on the Bestowal of the Five Blessings), also known as the *Qīngjìng Pínífāngděng Jīng* (Pure Vinaya Vaipulya Scripture); and one fascicle of the *Wúyōu Shījīng* (Scripture on the Bestowal of Freedom from Sorrow). There is also one fascicle of the *Āshéshìwáng Nǚ Míng Wújí Bǎosānmèi Jīng* (Scripture on the Samādhi of the Nameless Infinite Jewel of the Daughter of King Ajātaśatru). These were translated on the third day of the third month in the first year of the Yongjia era.
I have seen in the *Catalogue of Nie Daozhen* and its supplementary records the *Baowang Tongzi Jing* (Sūtra of the Jewel Net Boy) in one fascicle, also called the *Baowang Jing*.

I have seen in the *Catalogue of Nie Daozhen* the *Wenshushili Huiguo Jing* (Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Repentance) in one fascicle; it was first translated and also called the *Wenshushili Wuti Huiguo Jing* (Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Five-Part Repentance). I have seen the *Pufayi Jing* (Sūtra of the Universal Dharma Meaning) in one fascicle, also called the *Puyi Jing*; this second translation is largely the same with minor differences as that translated by An Shigao during the Han dynasty, according to the *Catalogue of Nie Daozhen*. I have seen the *Mie Shifang Ming Jing* (Sūtra on Extinguishing the Darkness of the Ten Directions) in one fascicle, which appeared on the fourteenth day of the eighth month of the Guangxi year.
One manuscript lacks the character "miè" (extinction).
I have seen a copy of the *Né Dàozhēn Lù Púsà Shí dì jīng* (Record by Né Dàozhēn of the Bodhisattva Ten Grounds Sūtra) in one fascicle,
which is also called the *Shí dì jīng* (Ten Grounds Sūtra) and also called the *Dà fāngguǎng jīng* (Mahāvaipulya Sūtra).
*Chūhōgon-juppokuhon-onshitsusenyoku-shūsōkyō* (The Scripture on Bathing the Assembly of Monks in a Warm Chamber from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Chapter on the Ten Stages), one fascicle;

also known as the *Onshikyō*. Recorded in the *Netsudōshinroku*. *Raishakwarashomon-kōtokutaishikyō* (The Scripture on Prince Kōtoku as Asked by Rāṣṭrapāla), one fascicle; issued on the thirtieth day of the ninth month in the sixth year of the Taishi era.

One volume titled *The Sūtra of Prince Guangde* (formerly known as *The Sūtra of the Prince of Radiant Virtue*), seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*. One volume titled *The Sūtra of Future Transformations*, seen in Nie Daozhen’s records. One volume titled *The Sūtra of the Five Hundred Disciples’ Own Accounts of Their Origins*, translated in the fifth month of the second year of the Taian era.
The *Jiulù* states: "The *Wǔbǎi dìzǐ shuō běnmò jīng* (Sūtra on the Exposition of the Origins by Five Hundred Disciples) is seen in the *Niè Dàozhēn Lù*.
It is one fascicle of the *Shīzǐyuè fóshēng jīng* (Sūtra on the Birth of the Buddha Śākyamuni), translated during the Dà'ān era."
I have seen one fascicle of the *Record of Kāśyapa’s Compilation and Transmission of the Sūtras* by Nie Daozhen; some say it is the *Compilation of the Vinaya Sūtra*.
I have also seen one fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Maiden Nanda and Jīvaka*, translated during the Taian era, as recorded by Nie Daozhen.
One title is *The Scripture of the Maiden Nāi*.
It is recorded in the *Nie Daozhen Lu* as one fascicle of the *Bao Tai Jing* (Scripture on the Womb), translated on the first day of the eighth month in the second year of the Taian era.
It is also called the *Bao Tai Shou Shen Jing* (Scripture on Receiving a Body in the Womb).
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* in one fascicle, recorded by Nie Daozhen, translated on the first day of the fourth month in the second year of the Taian era;
this is the third translation.

It is largely the same as, though with minor differences from, the version translated during the Han dynasty by Yan Fotiao and during the Wu dynasty by Zhi Qian; it is recorded in Nie Daozhen’s catalogue as *The Sūtra on the Questions of Ugraparipṛcchā Concerning the Bodhisattva Practice* in one fascicle, though some call it the *Ugra-gṛhapati-sūtra*.
This is the *Mahāyuga-sūtra*.
Alternatively, there is a two-fascicle version which is a third edition;
it is identical in content to the translations by Kang Seng Kai of the Wei period and Zhi Qian of the Wu period, though they differ in the degree of their textual elaboration or brevity.

The *Record* of Dao’an and Zhi Min-du lists one fascicle of the *Yanshi Renxian jing*; the *Record* of Nie Daozhen lists one fascicle of the *Jue zongchi jing* (also known as the *Jueding zongchi jing*); one fascicle of the *Shouyi nü jing* (also known as the *Fannü shouyi jing*); and one fascicle of the *Shatoujian jing* (also known as the *Taizi ershiba xiu jing*).
It is also called the *Hu’er yi jing* (Sūtra on the Meaning of the Tiger’s Ear).
It is a different translation from the same original text as the *Madengqie jing* (Mātṛkā Sūtra).
This is the second translation.
It differs slightly from the version translated by An Shigao during the Han dynasty.
According to Shi Dao’an’s catalogue, this *Dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpādasūtra* (one fascicle) is the third translation, alongside the one produced by An Shigao of the Han dynasty.

The Buddhist scriptures also mention the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination under the Pippala Tree* in one fascicle, also known as the *Brahmajāla Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views*, as recorded in Zhu Daozu’s catalogue. There is also the *Sūtra on Self-Inflicted Harm* in one fascicle, and the *Sūtra of the Silent Youth* in one or two fascicles, also known as the *Sūtra of the Silent Bodhisattva*.
Extracted from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*.
Recorded by Nie Daozhen as the *Śrīdharmamudrā-sūtra*, one fascicle. Extracted on the fifth day of the twelfth month of the fourth year of the Yuankang era at Jiuquan Commandery.
Zhu Fashou recorded it by brush.
It is also simply called the *Śrī-mudrā-sūtra* and is also called the *Prajñā-mudrā-sūtra*.
Dao’an stated that it is extracted from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
It is found in the records of Nie Daozhen and Baochang; there is one fascicle titled *Yishan jing* (Sutra on Moving Mountains), which the old records state: [end of quote].

*The Scripture of the Malla Moving the Mountain*, *The Scripture on the Pure and Adorned Samādhi*, one fascicle—also titled *The Scripture on the Introduction to the World*; *The Scripture of Wisdom and Clarity*, one fascicle; *The Scripture of Mahākāśyapa’s Original Vow*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta*, one fascicle. Translated during the Yuankang era.
It is also simply titled *The Sūtra on Avalokiteśvara Receiving Prediction*.

It is seen in Nie Daozhen’s catalog as *The Sūtra on the Merit of the Names of Buddhas in Various Directions*, one fascicle, and *The Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana Ascending to the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens*, one fascicle; in one version of the latter, the character "heaven" (天) is absent.

*Chūfó běnxíng jí jīng Pǔshǒu tóngzhēn jīng* (The Sutra on the Universal Chief Boyhood Deity from the Collection of the Buddha’s Original Acts), one fascicle; recorded in the catalogue of Niè Dàozhēn. *Shífāng fó míng jīng* (Sutra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions), one fascicle. *Sānpǐn xiūxíng jīng* (Sutra on the Practice of the Three Grades), also known as the *Sānpǐn huìguò jīng* (Sutra on the Repentance of the Three Grades).
Dao’an stated:

"In recent times, people have compiled the following scriptures: the *Jinyi Zhangzizi Jing* (Sutra of the Elder’s Son Jinyi) in one fascicle, the *Zhongyou Jing* (Sutra of the Multitude of Blessings) in one fascicle, the *Guangxing Buyi Sishi Jing* (Sutra on the Four Matters of Unwavering Contemplative Practice) in one fascicle, and the *Xiaofa Mojin Jing* (Sutra on the Exhaustion of the Lesser Dharma) in one fascicle."
The Sūtra of the Parable of the Four Wives, one fascicle; the Lu-yi-jen Sūtra, one fascicle;
the Sūtra of King Khaṇḍa, one fascicle; the Dānaya Sūtra, one fascicle;
the Nāgadatta Sūtra, one fascicle; and the Aśvarāja Sūtra, one fascicle.

*The Sūtra of the Deer Mother*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Virtue of Anāthapiṇḍada*, one fascicle (also known as *The Sūtra of the Clan of Anāthapiṇḍada*); *The Sūtra on the Brothers Nāga Kings Bestowing [Gifts] upon King Daśaśīla*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra of Exhorting and Transforming the King*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Names of One Hundred Buddhas*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on First Planting the Roots of All Merits*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra on the Fruits of the Śramaṇa’s Realization*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on Contemplating the Body*, one fascicle.
*Yiwang jing* (Sūtra of the King of Physicians), one fascicle; *Faguang jing* (Sūtra of Dharma Contemplation), one fascicle;
*Yijing* (Sūtra of Intention), one fascicle;
*Jianglong jing* (Sūtra on Subduing Dragons), one fascicle; *Yingfa jing* (Sūtra on Responding to the Dharma), one fascicle.
*Xiànjiàn jīng* (Sūtra on Wrong Views), one fascicle; *Hé kǔ jīng* (Sūtra on What is Suffering), one fascicle;
*Shòusuì jīng* (Sūtra on Observing the Uposatha), one fascicle; *Pīnqióng jīng* (Sūtra on Poverty), one fascicle;

*Guànlà jīng* (Sūtra on the Ritual of Offering Cakes), one fascicle—also known as the *Bānníhuán hòu sìbèi guànlà jīng* (Sūtra on the Ritual of Offering Cakes by the Four Classes after the Parinirvāṇa); *Mìjù jīng* (Sūtra on Secret Provisions), one fascicle; *Chūshēng jīng* (Sūtra on Birth).
*The Sūtra on Repentance*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sūtra on Śāriputra’s Repentance for Transgressions*, one fascicle;
*The Sūtra on the Dharma Society*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Miscellaneous Praises with Explanatory Notes*, one fascicle (according to the secular commentary);
*The Ullambana Sūtra*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Differentiation*, one fascicle.

Three hundred and thirty-five fascicles;
these are all from the old catalogs and the *Sanzang ji*. From the one-fascicle *Duowen jing* (Sutra of Much Hearing) below, there are forty-eight works comprising forty-eight fascicles.

Slightly differing from those produced by Dharmadhara, [this] is one fascicle of the *Zhongjing lumu* (Catalogue of Various Scriptures).
The above totals two hundred and ten works, comprising three hundred and ninety-four fascicles.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi country.
Dharmarakṣa (translated into Chinese as Fahu) was originally surnamed Zhi.
He traveled extensively throughout the Western Regions, mastering the languages and scripts of thirty-six countries.
From the kingdom of India, he brought with him a great quantity of Sanskrit manuscripts of the Brahmanical scriptures and arrived at the Jade Gate.
Thereupon, he resided in Dunhuang.
Consequently, he was known as Zhushi.
Later, he arrived in Luoyang and traveled to Jiangzuo,
beginning from the first year of the Taishi era during the reign of Emperor Wu.
During the reign of Emperor Huai, in the second year of the Yongjia era,
whenever he encountered favorable conditions in his various locations, he translated scriptures with the lay devotee Nie Chengyuan taking up the pen to assist in the translation;
the resulting volumes were most numerous.
However, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states only that Saṃghavarman produced one hundred and sixty-five works;
whereas Sengyou’s *Collection of Records of the Tripitaka* (*Sanzang jiji*) records only one hundred and fifty-four works in three hundred and nine fascicles.
Among these, the catalog compiled by Shi Dao'an lacks four sections, which Sengyou has supplied.
Dao'an said:
Having encountered an era of turmoil, the catalogues were scattered like stars;
that they have become intermingled with one another is indeed the case.
This is why there are miscellaneous records and various separate chronicles.
It is recorded that many [versions] were translated by Zhu Fahu;
thus we know that what has now been obtained is certainly the translation of Master Hu (Fahu), without any doubt.
Therefore, Nie Chengyuan’s son Daozhen, together with Zhu Fashou, Chen Shilun, Sun Bohu, Yu Shi, and others, [collated it].
Those who transcribed both the preceding and following sections have already appeared in separate biographies,
so they will not be recorded here in detail. Furthermore,
there are Li Kuò’s Record and the Miscellaneous Separate Record.
It further states that Bodhisattva Zhi translated six works totaling sixteen fascicles.
Sengyou’s catalogue records that these were translated by a Bodhisattva from India.
The number [of fascicles] is the same as in the *Qunlu* (Collection of Records), differing only in their titles;
however, the commentary appended below by Sengyou states that it was translated jointly by Zhi Qian and Zhu Fahu.
According to the *Jian* (the *Gaoseng zhuan*), the name is translated as *Dharmaraksita*,
which in the Jin language means "Dharma-protector" (*Fahu*).
Nevertheless, the titles of the six scriptures translated by Master Zhi are all included within Dharmarakṣa’s catalog.
The surnames "Zhi" and "Zhu" differ in their origins and endings;
the term "Bodhisattva" is merely a honorific title used to praise them.
Upon examining various records, it is clear that the Bodhisattva Zhi was none other than Zhu Fahu.
There are not two separate persons;
the *Chusanzangji* (Record of the Tripitaka Translations) treats them as two distinct instances,
which is not a careful or thorough analysis.
2. *Jiangliang louzhi shieryou jing* (The Scripture on the Twelve Wanderings of Jiangliang Louzhi), one fascicle.
This single scripture was [translated] during the reign of Emperor Wu by the foreign śramaṇa Jiangliang Louzhi.
The Jin term is *zhēn-xǐ* (True Joy).
It was translated in Guangzhou during the second year of the Taishi era.
This is recorded in the Shixing lu and the Baochang lu.
3. *Anfǎqīn Dà Ayùwáng jīng* (The Great Aśoka Sūtra Spoken by An Faqin), five fascicles;

translated during the Guangxī era. It appears in Zhūdózú’s *Jìnshì zá lù*. *Dàoshénzú Wújí biànhuà jīng* (Sūtra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of Dao Shen), two fascicles; second translation.
It is also available in three or four fascicles;

The text differs slightly from that seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin shi za lu*. The *Wenshushili xian baozang jing* (Mañjuśrī’s Manifestation of the Treasure Store Sūtra) in two fascicles was translated in the second year of the Taian era;
it is also found in three fascicles.

It is also called the *Xianbaozang jing* (Sutra on Manifesting the Treasure Store); see Zhu Daozu’s *Jin shi zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty). The *Ajase wang jing* (Sutra of King Ajātaśatru) in two fascicles was translated during the Taikang era;

see Zhu Daozu’s *Jin shi zalu*. The *Anan mugua jing* (Sutra of Ānanda Mukha) in one fascicle shares the same name but a different text from the *Weimi chi jing* (Sutra of the Subtle and Secret Retention).
I have seen in *Zhu Daozu’s Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* that there was a work titled *Mufa* (Dharmamati) in five sections totaling twelve fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Hui,
the Śramaṇa An Faqin from the country of Anxi [translated it].
Translated at Luoyang during the Taikang era. 4.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Fàngguāng bōrě jīng) in twenty fascicles; the third translation by Mokṣala (Zhu Shixing).

This work is identical in its original text to the *Daoxing* and *Xiaopin* translated by Zhu Foshuo during the Han dynasty, though it is a separate translation with a different title. It consists of one section comprising twenty fascicles.
This sutra was originally [procured] by Zhu Shixing of Yingchuan.
I examined a separate copy of it;
while traveling in Luoyang, he once lectured on the *Dàoxíng* [Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra].
Upon reading it, I privately perceived that its phrasing was obscure and substantial, with certain aspects that were not entirely excellent.
Every time he sighed in lamentation, he would say:
"This sutra is truly the essence of the Mahāyāna;
yet its text has not been fully translated, and its principles remain incomplete."
Vowing to sacrifice his own body, he resolved to seek it out.
Setting out from Yongzhou in the fifth year of the Gānlù era at the end of the Wei dynasty,
he eventually traveled to the Western Regions.
In the kingdom of Khotan, he obtained the aforementioned Sanskrit manuscript consisting of ninety chapters,
totaling less than six hundred thousand words.
He dispatched his disciple Pūrṇatāra.
The Jin dynasty records that he was named Fara (法饒).
He was sent back from Khotan to Luoyang.
Before his departure, the various monks and followers of the Hīnayāna school in Khotan...
He then informed the King, saying:
"A Han śramaṇa wishes to use Brahmanic script to confuse and disorder the orthodox scriptures.
Your Majesty is the lord of the earth."
"If you do not prohibit this, the Great Dharma will be severed and the land of Han will be left deaf and blind;
this would be the King's fault.
The King then refused to allow the scriptures to be taken beyond his borders.
Shixing was deeply distressed and harbored a heart of profound sorrow;
he then requested permission to burn the sutra as proof,
and the king granted his request immediately.
Thereupon, they piled up firewood and placed it before the palace, intending to burn him.
When the Master arrived, he stood before the flames with utmost sincerity and took an oath, saying:
"If the Great Dharma is destined to flow into the land of Han..."
"The sutra should not be so.
If it does not protect my life, what is the use?
Having said this, he threw the sutra away.
The fire was immediately extinguished;
the parchment remained as it was before,
appearing even more radiant and fresh.
The great assembly was struck with awe and submitted, all acclaiming it as a divine response.
Consequently, he was able to send [the scriptures] on, and they reached Chenliu.
There, he again encountered the Khotanese monks Zhu Foshuo, Wuluocha, and Zhu Shulan.
It was translated on the tenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Yuankang era during the reign of Emperor Hui at the South Temple by the Cangheng River.
This is recorded in the various catalogs compiled by Zhu Daozu, Sengyou, Wang Zong, Baochang, Li Kuò, Fashang, Lingyu, and others.
The catalogs of various scriptures all state that Zhu Shixing translated this;
this is likely because the person who originally sought it out attributed the merit to him.

The *Fáng shěn kǎn zhī Míndù lù* (Fáng’s Collated Record of Zhī Míndù), the *Gāosēng chuán chūjīng hòujì* (Biographies of Eminent Monks: Postscript on the Translation of Scriptures), and various miscellaneous catalogs were all meticulously translated by the three masters Vimalākṣa, Zhu Shulan, and others.
Zhu Shixing remained in Khotan and passed away there;
he sent only his disciples to carry the scriptures to the land of Jin.
How could this be called the "Emergence of the Conduct of a Scholar"? 5.
*Niet Chengyuan Chao Riming Sanmei Jing* (The Sutra on the Sun-Transcending Radiance Samādhi), two fascicles; the second translation.
It is also simply called the *Chao Riming Jing*.
It is largely the same as, yet slightly different from, the three-fascicle version previously translated by Zhu Fahu.
It is the second translation of the *Kāśyapa-aniruddha-sūtra* (or *Kāśyapa-questions-to-Ananda-sūtra*),

The *Yue nan jing* (Sutra on Overcoming Difficulties), one fascicle, second edition, as recorded in the *Shixing lu* and the *Baochang lu*. The above three sutras comprise four fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor Hui, the lay devotee and upāsaka Nie Chengyuan [compiled them].
Although these sutras and others were all translated earlier,
their phrasing and meaning were obscure and substantial, and their logical sentences were not yet perfected.
Much later, they were therefore reorganized and reformulated into verses, with the revisions surpassing those of the previous versions.
It is that which is currently being practiced in the world. 6.

*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* translated by Zhu Shulan in three fascicles; this fifth edition from the sixth year of Yuankang is largely identical with minor differences to the versions translated during the Han dynasty by Yan Fotiao, during the Wu dynasty by Zhi Qian, Zhu Fahu, and Kumārajīva.
Alternatively, it consists of two fascicles.
According to the *Zhudaozu lu*, the two-fascicle *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* was translated in the first year of the Yuankang era;
this is the fifth translation.

The two sections translated by Zhu Fahu and Zhu Shulan differ in wording but are identical in substance; this is seen in the *Zhēnlù* (Record of Authenticity). These two scriptures comprise five fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor Hui, the Western Region śramaṇa Zhu Shulan translated them both in Luoyang.

Nie Chengyuan’s son, Daozhen,

During the reign of Emperor Hui,
the śramaṇa Bai Fazhu of Henan produced [the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*].

However, because the various sutras produced during that period encountered a time of turmoil and upheaval, their catalogs have rarely survived;
thus, their true extent remains unrecorded.
Daofang extensively searched through various miscellaneous records.
Having examined these twenty-two sutras,
all of which are annotated as having been produced by the Patriarch,
I have now recorded them in full according to what I have observed.

During the reign of Emperor Hui, the śramaṇa Shi Falì, together with Faju and others, translated [this] at Luoyang.

This is seen in the *Jin shi zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) by Zhu Daozu. The above is one sūtra in two fascicles.

During the reign of Emperor Hui,

It is also titled the *Gṛhapati-vinaya-sūtra*, or simply the *Vinaya-sūtra*;

it is also called the *Bodhisattva-gati-sūtra* or simply the *Gati-sūtra*. These five versions are largely identical, differing only in their separate translations and distinct titles. The two separate records of the Wu [dynasty] are both direct, standalone annotations.
They appeared during the Yuankang era;
the translators are not specified.
Having examined the various catalogs in detail, I have not yet found a definitive attribution.
Consequently, this separate item remains distinct and its translator is lost.
From the *Lìdài sānbǎo jì*, Volume Six: Translations of the Western Jin Dynasty.
4. Translation of Scriptures (Eastern Jin). *Lìdài sānbǎo jì*, Scroll Seven: Records of Scripture Translation during the Eastern Jin.
Submitted by the Subject Fèi Chángfáng, Academician for Scripture Translation, in the seventeenth year of the Kāiyuán era.
Regarding the Record of the Eastern Jin: He was a great-grandson of Emperor Xuán, a descendant of Wǔwáng of Lángyá, and the son of Gōngwáng Jǐn.
His son was named Rui, with the style name Jingwen.
On the morning of his birth, a divine light appeared within the room, illuminating it entirely.
A white hair grew from the left corner of his eye;
his eyes possessed a brilliant luster, and his gaze was majestic and radiant.

He held successive offices, serving as General Who Wields Martial Authority on Behalf of the State (Shichijie), General Who Guards the East (Andong Jiangjun), Commander-in-Chief of all Military Affairs in Yangzhou (Dudu Yangzhou Zhunjun Shi), and Left Chancellor (Zuo Xianghuang).
After the defeat of Emperor Hui and Emperor Min, the officials were scattered;
some fled to the south of the Yangtze River,
while others were slaughtered by Shi Le.
When Chang’an fell and the Emperor was held captive in Pingyang,
five hundred subordinates suddenly appeared in Jiangdong and urged Fu Rong that he should style himself Prince of Jin,
take charge of all affairs of state, and preside over the millions of subjects.
After the Emperor Min passed away, he subsequently ascended the throne;
he styled his reign the first year of Jianwu and established his capital at Jianye.
It was changed to Jiankang to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Min.
Previously, in the second year of Taikang, Guan Gong, a former general of Wu, incited a rebellion.
At that time, Wu Zhen of Jianye performed a divination for him, saying:
"Gongyi has already passed away.
However, after thirty-eight years,
there shall be an Emperor in Yangzhou."
When this occurred, it was indeed just as he had said.
Furthermore, during the reign of the First Emperor of Qin,
a diviner of vapors declared that within five hundred years, a Son of Heaven would emerge from Mount Jinling in Wu.
The First Emperor feared this;
he dispatched troops and excavated Mount Jinling, renaming it Moleling,
in the hope of severing its royal connection.
From the first year of the Zhengshi era of the Jin dynasty until the two hundred and sixth year,
the Jin, with its metal mandate, suddenly ruled the four seas;
it was at this time that the auspicious signs of Jinling appeared.
Furthermore, a popular song says:
"Five horses floated across the river;
one horse transformed into a dragon."
During the chaos and upheaval of the Yongjia era, the empire fell into ruin;
only the five princes of Langya, Xiyang, Runan, Nandun, and Pengcheng managed to find refuge south of the Yangtze River.
Among them, Wang Rui was the first to establish a foundation, serving as the primary minister to Emperor Yuan.

It is known that the mandate received above moved the celestial spirits to desire the crossing over and the establishment of a grand design, while below it relied upon the geomantic power of the earth;
the earth bore its potential, which the First Emperor attempted to excavate but could not destroy,
and Heaven bestowed its spiritual power.
Liu Yao annihilated them, yet they were not entirely exterminated.
From the first year of the Jianwu era of Emperor Yuan (dingchou) when the capital was established,
until the first year of the Yuanxi era of Emperor Gong (jǐwèi) when the mandate was ceded to the Song dynasty.
During that interval of one hundred and forty years,
twenty-seven individuals— both Chinese and non-Chinese, monastics and laypeople—
produced translated scriptures, including those whose original translators had been lost.
In total, there are two hundred and sixty-three works comprising five hundred and eighty-five fascicles;
these are compiled as the *Jiankang Lu* (Record of Jiankang) for the twelve rulers of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The Śramaṇa Śrīmitra of the Eastern Jin translated eleven fascicles of sūtras and dhāraṇīs from three sections;
the Śramaṇa Zhidao Gen translated seven fascicles of sūtras from two sections;
and the Śramaṇa Kang Fasuì [translated one section].
One scripture in ten fascicles by the śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan;
one hundred and one scriptures and dhāraṇīs totaling one hundred and twelve fascicles; one scripture in three fascicles by the śramaṇa Kang Daohuo;
and [scriptures] by the śramaṇa Kalodayin.
One scripture in one fascicle by the śramaṇa Saṃghadeva;
one hundred and seventeen scriptures and treatises in five fascicles by the śramaṇa Vimalākṣa;
and two sections on miscellaneous matters of the Vinaya in five fascicles by the śramaṇa Dharma.
One work in two fascicles: *Lüyào* (Essentials of the Vinaya), by the śramaṇa Buddhavarman;
fifteen works in one hundred and fifteen fascicles: scriptures, precepts, treatises, and biographies, by the śramaṇa Faxian;
six works in twenty-four fascicles: scriptures, precepts, treatises, and biographies, by the śramaṇa Jīvaka.
Twenty-five scriptures in forty-six fascicles by the foreign lay devotee Zhu Nanti;
two scriptures in three fascicles by the śramaṇa Shi Fali;
and one scripture in one fascicle by the śramaṇa Shi Sengong.
One work in three fascicles by the śramaṇa Shi Tui-gong;
one work in one fascicle by the śramaṇa Shi Fa-yong;
one work in one fascicle by the śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan.
Fourteen works in thirty-five fascicles: *Śāstra in Praise of the Śramaṇa* by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengfu, one work in one fascicle;
*Treatise* by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanshen, two works in six fascicles;
*Commentary on the Treatise* by the Śramaṇa Zhi Dun.
*Zhiguī* (Aims and Conclusions) in seven sections and seven fascicles by the śramaṇa Zhu Sengdu;
one section and one fascicle. *Zhiguī* by the śramaṇa Shi Daozu in four sections and four fascicles. Catalogue by the śramaṇa Zhi Mindu.
One fascicle, one volume: *Dulu* (General Catalog), by the śramaṇa Kang Fachang;
one fascicle, one volume: *Lun* (Treatise), by the śramaṇa Zhu Faji;

The doctrinal purport of the two sections and two fascicles is as follows:

fifty-three sūtras and dhāraṇīs in fifty-seven fascicles translated during the Eastern Jin dynasty by various unknown translators, totaling fifty-three works in fifty-seven fascicles. 1. *The Sūtra of the Consecration of Śrīmitra* (9 fascicles), seen in the *Zalu*. 2. *The Great Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī Dhāraṇī Sūtra* (1 fascicle), seen in Zhu Daozu’s *Jinshi Zalu* and the *Sanzang Ji*. 3. *The Miscellaneous Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī Dhāraṇī Sūtra* (1 fascicle), also seen in Zhu Daozu’s records; however, the translation is incomplete.
Together with the *Sanzang ji* (Record of the Tripitaka), these two sections comprise eleven fascicles in total.
During the era of Emperor Yuan,
there was the Śramaṇa from the Western Regions, Śrīmitra.
In the language of Jin, he was called Jiyou.
He was the son of a king who,
being destined to inherit the throne, yielded the kingdom to his younger brother.
At An’gui, Taibo awakened to the mind within and was thus initiated as a śramaṇa.
His natural bearing was lofty and bright, and his spirit and demeanor were exceptionally refined and transcendent.
To face it directly is,
in itself, already to stand out prominently,
transcending all phenomena.
How much more so for those who were eloquent and capable of engaging in dialogue?
When Prime Minister Wang Dao saw him once,
he marveled at him and considered him one of his own kind.
Because of this, he became renowned by that name.
Dao once said to Mi,
"In foreign lands, there is only you, one such person."
Mili smiled and replied,
"If I were like you, O donor,
how could I have traveled here today?"
The people of the time considered this an excellent response.
He was adept at maintaining incantations and mantras, which proved effective in every instance;
his teachings flourished throughout Jiankang.
The people of that time called him the Dharma Master of the High Seat (Gaozuo Fashi).
He also taught his disciples the *Mili* and the loud chanting of Buddhist hymns (*fanbai*),

Dao’an was originally a native of Fuliu in Changshan;
his secular surname was Wei.
His family lineage had produced many eminent scholars.
Having lost his parents early, he was raised by his maternal uncle, the Kong family.
At the age of seven, when he read a book, he could recite it after reading it only once.
His neighbors marveled at this extraordinary change.
When he reached the age of twelve, he left the household life;
his spiritual nature was sharp and quick-witted, yet his physical appearance was extremely unattractive.
He was not held in high esteem by his teacher;
yet he performed manual labor and service without ever showing a trace of resentment.
By nature steadfast and diligent, he observed the fasts and precepts without fail.
Several years later, he finally approached his teacher to request a scripture.
The teacher gave him one fascicle of the *Bianyi jing* (Sūtra on Resolving Doubts),
consisting of approximately five thousand words.
An carried the sutra into the fields;
while resting there, he took the opportunity to read it.
At dusk, he returned and gave the sutra back to his teacher.
When he sought something else,
the teacher said,
"Yesterday you did not read the sutra; why do you seek it again today?"
After Ananda had finished reciting the sutra,
although his teacher marveled at it,
he did not yet believe it.
Furthermore, he brought with him one fascicle of the Chengju guangming jing (Sūtra of Perfect Radiance),
comprising slightly less than ten thousand words,
carrying it just as he had done before.
At dusk, he returned to his teacher;
the teacher held up the scripture to test him, and he did not err by even a single character.
The teacher was greatly amazed and marveled at him, regarding him with profound respect and wonder.
Later, he received full ordination and was permitted to travel freely for study during the reigns of Emperors Huai and Min of the Jin dynasty.
While fleeing to the west and east, he first encountered Fotudeng.

Dao’an often remarked that translating from the Hu language into the Qin language involves five points where the original is lost and three points where it is difficult not to alter.
The first is that the Hu language is entirely inverted in structure, yet it must be made to conform to the Qin;
this is the first loss of the original.
Second, the Hu scriptures value substance while the people of Qin favor elegance;
to transmit [the teachings] so as to accord with the hearts of the masses, elegance is indispensable.
This second point constitutes a departure from the original.
Third, the Hu scriptures are exhaustive and detailed, proceeding with such earnestness and repetition that they may be chanted three or four times without deeming the text too prolix;
yet now you have abridged and excised them.
The third is a loss of the original.
Fourth, as for the so-called "explanations of meaning," they closely resemble disordered speech;
upon examining the preceding words, there is no difference in their phrasing.
Whether it be one thousand or five hundred,
they are cut down and no longer exist;
this is the fourth loss of the root.
Fifth, when matters are combined for presentation and one intends to branch out into further discussion,
yet instead reverts to citing previous statements and subsequently explains them, thereby completely omitting the original substance—
this is the fifth loss of the original.
However, although wisdom penetrates the mind of the threefold transcendence,
the holy teachings manifested by the Buddha must necessarily accord with the times;
for worldly customs are subject to change.
To prune the refined and ancient to suit the present age is the first thing that cannot be changed.
The gap between the foolish and the wise is as vast as heaven and earth; even a sage cannot bridge it.
To wish to transmit the subtle words from a thousand years ago so that they accord with the vulgar customs of the later ages of a hundred kings—
this is the second difficulty.
Ānanda produced the scriptures not long after the Buddha’s passing.
The venerable Mahākāśyapa commanded five hundred arhats possessing the six supernormal powers to examine one another and record [the teachings] in turn.

That those in the cycle of birth and death remain so indifferent and ordinary—

This is the third difficulty.
Having traversed these five losses and three difficulties,
one translates from the Hu language into Qin.

During the night, someone pulled the *Chen* (the scripture) down to the ground.

After three such nights,

"What is this used for as a pillow?
Chen then felt ashamed and awakened to the truth;

Delightedly observing that Mingneng could pose questions and challenges with such mastery,

The Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci (translated as Fǎxī in Wei) from South India translated [this work] at Luoyang for Emperor Xuánwǔ.
Sāṃghika Śramaṇa Dàobǎo received [the dictation] with the brush. 2.
*Dharmabhāṇaka Byañjaka-putra Gṛhapati-paripṛcchā Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as the *Gṛhapati Byañjaka Sūtra*. The above is one work in one fascicle.
During the Tianjian era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
the Northern Wei śramaṇa Shi Fachang produced [this work] in Luoyang.
I have consulted the *Shamen Fashang Lu* (Record of Dharma-upholding Śramaṇas).

Volume 3: *Bodhiruci’s Foming Jing* (Sūtra of Buddha Names), twelve fascicles; translated during the Zhengguang era. *Lengqie Jing* (Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra), ten fascicles; translated in the second year of the Yanchang era.
This is the second edition.
It differs from the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* translated by Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty, as it provides a more extensive explanation.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-śāṭhyāyana-putra-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* in ten fascicles was transcribed by the śramaṇas Senglang and Daozhan in the first year of the Zhengguang era.
In Luoyang, he served as the Governor of Sizhou and Prince of Runan; this is the second edition.
Alternatively, the *Dharmasaṃgraha-sūtra* in seven or eight fascicles was translated in Luoyang in the fourth year of the Yanchang era.
Senglang received it in writing.

Alternatively, there is a six-fascicle version recorded in Fashang’s catalogue; this *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in six fascicles was translated at Luoyang in the first year of the Shenggui era.
This is the third translation.

The six-fascicle *Cittadhāraṇī-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty and the four-fascicle *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* (or *Samparigraha-sūtra*) translated by Kumārajīva during the Qin dynasty are different translations of the same original text;
this is recorded in the *Fashang lu*. Furthermore, the five-fascicle *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* [was translated] in the third year of the Yanchang era.
In Luoyang, it was translated with Sengbian acting as the scribe.
It is recorded in Fashang’s catalogue as the second translation of the *Vīradattaparipṛcchā-sūtra* in two fascicles;

this is a different recension from the *Īśvararāja-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva during the Qin dynasty, though they share the same source text. Also, the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta-sūtra* in two fascicles was translated in Luoyang during the Zhengguang era.
Alternatively, there is one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle, translated in the second year of the Yongping era at the residence of the State Councilor Hu.
This is the second edition;
Senglang received it by dictation.

This differs slightly from the version translated by Kumārajīva during the Qin dynasty; it is recorded in Fǎshàng’s catalogue. *The Sūtra on the Prophecy of Kṣemadatta*, one fascicle, translated in Luoyang during the Zhengguang era with Sēnglǎng as the scribe. *The Sūtra of the Buddha’s Words*, one fascicle, with Sēnglǎng as the scribe. *The Sūtra of the Jewel Casket Without Letters*, one fascicle, with Sēnglǎng as the scribe. *The Sūtra on Entering the Seal of Non-attainment*, one fascicle, with Juéyì as the scribe. *The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, one fascicle, second translation.

The *Sūtra on the Turning of Existence* (Yǔ zhuǎn yǒu jīng), one fascicle, is a different translation from the same original as [the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*]. The *Sūtra on the Essential Wisdom of the Mahāyāna* (Yǔ dàchéng yào huì jīng) is a separate edition from the same original.
Both were translated at the residence of Zhao Xin.
*The Scripture on the Supreme Dharma of the Pen-reception of the Awakened Mind*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Peak of Gayā*, one fascicle, translated for the second time.
These share the same original text as the *Bodhi Sūtra* by Kumārajīva of the Qin dynasty, though they have been separately issued under different titles.

*The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Perambulation*, one fascicle, transcribed by Senglang; *The Scripture on the High King of All Dharmas*, one fascicle, transcribed by Jueyi (same text as the *Scripture on the Heroic King of All Dharmas*, translated under a different title); *The Dhāraṇī Scripture for Protecting All Children*, one fascicle; *The Treatise on the Ratnakūṭa Scripture*, four fascicles; *The Scripture on Slandering the Buddha*, one fascicle, second edition.
This is a different translation from the same original text as the *Niścaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty, though it bears a distinct title;
it is also simply called the *Niścaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. The twelve-fascicle *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* was recorded in Li Kuò’s catalogue.
The initial translation was personally received by Emperor Xuanwu from his own hand one day in the Great Hall;
it was only later, in the first year of the Putai era, that it was finalized and entrusted to the śramaṇa Sengbian as the ten-fascicle *Suvikrāntavikrāmi-paripṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*.
The *Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtraśāstra* in ten fascicles was produced at the residence of Yuan Taoyang in Luoyang, with Senglang and Sengbian acting as scribes.

The *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrāsūtraśāstra* in four fascicles and the *Vajracchedikāprajñāpāramitāsūtraśāstra* in three fascicles were produced at the residence of Zhao Xin in Luoyang in the second year of the Yongping era, with Senglang acting as the scribe.
In the second year of the Tiānpíng era, at the residence of Minister Hu Xiāng, the *Gayaśīrṣa-sūtra-śāstra* in two fascicles was produced with Sēnglǎng serving as scribe.

At Bānzhòu Monastery in Yèchéng, the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-śāstra* in one fascicle (also known as the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra*) was produced, with Sēngbiàn and Dàozhàn serving as scribes. The *Anupūrva-madhyama-śāstra* in two fascicles was produced with Cúì Guāng, the Palace Attendant, serving as scribe. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* in two fascicles was produced with Tánlín serving as scribe and composing the preface. The *Tripariśuddha-sūtra-śāstra* in one fascicle was translated in the fifth year of the Shùnshǐ era, with Cúì Guāng, the Palace Attendant, serving as scribe. The *Amitāyur-upadeśa-sūtra-śāstra* in one fascicle was produced in the first year of the Pútài era.

*The Bodhisattva Ratnacūḍa’s Discourse on the Four Dharmas*, one fascicle, transcribed by Sengbian; *The Treatise on the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma*, one fascicle, transcribed by Tanlin; *The Treatise on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, one fascicle; *The Treatise on the Hundred Letters*, one fascicle; *The Treatise Refuting the Four Tenets of the Heretics*, one fascicle; *The Treatise Refuting the Nirvāṇa of the Heretics*, one fascicle; and *The Catalogue of Translated Scriptures and Treatises*, one fascicle. The above total comprises thirty-eight works, amounting to one hundred and twenty-seven fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
there was the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci from North India,
who in Wei was called Daohui.
From the second year of the Yongping era of the Wei dynasty until the Tianping era,
a period spanning more than twenty years,
he translated [the scriptures] while residing in Luoyang and Ye.
Li Kuò’s record states that there were originally ten thousand fascicles (*jia*) of Brahmanical sūtras and śāstras within the Tripiṭaka Master’s quarters;
the manuscript copies of the sūtras and śāstras he translated filled an entire room.
However, his wisdom and understanding were nearly equal to those of Ratnamati, and he was exceptionally quick-witted.
He was thoroughly proficient in local dialects and skilled in various arts;
once, he sat inside an empty alms-bowl at the mouth of a well.
The disciples were not yet present,
and there was no one to draw water;
the Tripitaka Master then took a willow branch and lightly swept the mouth of the well with it.
As he silently recited the mantra just a few times,
the spring surged upward until it reached the rim of the well;
the Tripitaka Master then immediately drew water from it with his alms bowl.
When the monks nearby saw this, they all sighed in admiration and praised him as a sage.
The Dharma Master then said,
"This is a magical art practiced commonly in foreign lands."
In this land, those who have not practiced these methods claim they are "holy";
fearing that they might delude the people of the world,
they consequently cause the mixing of various dharmas.
All were kept secret and not practiced. 4.

*Lènmó tí píyēshā wèn jīng* (The Sūtra on the Questions of Lènmó tí and Píyēshā), two fascicles; *Lóngshù púsà hé xiāng fāng* (The Incense Formula of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna), one fascicle—altogether fifty dharmas. *Shí dì jīng lùn* (Treatise on the Ten Stages Sūtra), twelve fascicles: when this treatise was first translated, the Wei language had not yet been mastered.
He had previously referred to the world of vessels as the "world of bowls.
Later, while entering the hall for a meal, he saw several venerable elders;
when he asked his disciples for a vessel, they all handed him their alms-bowls and bags.
Realizing that "receptacle" (*bhājana*) was a collective designation, he subsequently revised it;
the resulting *Baoji jing lun* (Treatise on the Jewel Accumulation Scripture) in four fascicles—both of these treatises were translated by Bodhiruci.
Furthermore, as the two masters vied for renown, they did not consult one another;
consequently, there were hidden discrepancies and mutual differences between them, leading to variations even in the phrasing of their written texts.
It was only later that these were synthesized.
The *Bǎochàng lù* records that there is a four-fascicle version of the *Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra*, also titled the *Ratnagotra-vibhāga-saptayānottara-śāstra*,
or alternatively a three-fascicle version.
Produced at the residence of Zhao Xin;

one fascicle of the *Dharmapada-sūtra-śāstra* (Fǎhuá jīng lùn) recorded by Bǎochàng, with the Palace Attendant Cui Guang acting as scribe. Altogether, these six sections comprise twenty-four fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
there was the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati (also known as Bodhi) from the kingdom of Central India.
The Wei language term for this is *Ratnamati*.
He arrived at the palace in Luoyang in the fifth year of the Zhengshi era to serve as a translator.
Initially, Bodhiruci assisted in the transmission.
Later, due to disagreements, these were translated separately by different individuals.
The śramaṇa Senglang, Jueyi, and Cui Guang, the Palace Attendant, served as scribes.

1. *Buddhāsaṃtada-jingang-samādhi-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle. 2. *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, one fascicle. The above two sūtras appeared in the sixth year of the Zhengguang era. 3. *Zhuanyou jing* (Sūtra on the Transformation of Existence), one fascicle. 4. *Shifa jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Dharmas), one fascicle. 5. *Yinse nü jing* (Sūtra of the Silver-Colored Woman), one fascicle. 6. *Zhengfa gongjing jing* (Sūtra on Reverencing the True Dharma), one fascicle; alternatively, it may lack the character "fa" (dharma).

Also known as the *Weide tuoluoni zhong shuo jing wuwei de nü jing* (Sūtra Spoken within the *Oṣadhiprabhāsa-dhāraṇī* on the Virtuous Woman Fearless), one fascicle; this is a different translation from the same original text as the *Ashudabosha jing*.
Transcribed by Tanlin. The *Wuzi baoqie jing* (Sūtra of the Jewel Casket of No Letters), one fascicle. These are the six sūtras mentioned above.

In the second year of the Yuánxiàng era, he translated the *Ānàduómùqié níhélí tuóluóní jīng* (Anantamukhanirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra), one fascicle; this was a separate translation of the same text as the five sūtras including the *Zhīqián wúliàng wēīmì chí bátuóluóní* (Kṣemaṅkara’s *Aparimitāyur-jñāna-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī*), the *Wúliàngmén chí gōngdé zhí wúliàngmén pómó tuóluóní* (Aparimitāyur-jñāna-nāma-dhāraṇī), and the *Shèlìfú tuóluóní* (Śāriputra-dhāraṇī). He also translated the *Shè dàchéng lùn* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra), two fascicles, during the first year of the Pǔtài era. Altogether, these comprise ten works totaling eleven fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, there was the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas from the kingdom of North India;
"Buddhayaśas" means "Awakened Stability" (Jue-ding) in the Wei language.
From the sixth year of the Zhengguang era to the second year of the Yuanxiang era,

at Baima Monastery in Luoyang and Jinhua Monastery in the capital of Ye, [the following was translated]: the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* in seventy fascicles by Gautama Prajñāruci, translated in the first year of the Xinghe era during the Northern Wei dynasty in the capital of Ye.
Translated at the residence of the Grand Chancellor Gao Cheng in Ye City.
Transcribed by Tanlin, Sengfang, and others.
*The Scripture on the Questions of the Holy Devaputra Susthitamati*, three fascicles. The third year of the Xinghe era.
Produced at Jinhua Monastery in Ye City.

This is a different translation from the *Mahāsāṃnipāta-sūtra* (translated by Dharmarakṣa) based on the same original text, with the alternative title *The Sutra of the Eight Buddhas*, transcribed by Tanlin. One fascicle. *The Sutra of the Golden-Colored King*. One fascicle. These two preceding sutras were both produced at Jinhua Monastery in the fourth year of the Xinghe era.

One fascicle of the *Vimalā-dārikā-sūtra* was transcribed by pen by Tánlín; it was produced in the third year of the Xìnghé era. One fascicle of the *Vimalā-upāsikā-sūtra* was produced in the fourth year of the Xìnghé era. One fascicle of the *Ratnamati-mārjāra-sūtra* was produced at Jīnhuá Monastery for Gāo Zhònmì. One fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-caturdharma-sūtra* was produced at Jīnhuá Monastery.
One fascicle of the *Vinayamātṛkā-śīla-sūtra* (Jiětuō jièběn), transcribed by Tánlín, Lǐ Yìxī, and others;
produced in the second year of the Xīnghé era.
One fascicle of the *Kāśyapīya-vinaya-Śākya-bhikṣu-praśna-śāstra* (Jiāshèpí lǜdúzǐ dàorén wèn lùn), transcribed by Sēngfǎng; produced at Jīnhuá Temple for Gāo Zhòngmì.
*Huisheng lun* (Treatise on Turning Back Disputes), one fascicle; transcribed by Li Yixi, issued in the first year of the Yuangxiang era.
*Ye chengjiu lun* (Treatise on the Accomplishment of Practice), one fascicle; transcribed by Tanlin, [issued] in the third year of the Xinghe era.
Produced at Jinhua Temple, with Tanlin serving as scribe:

*The Treatise on Consciousness-only Without Objects* (one fascicle), also known as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*; and the *Ekāṣṭaka-śloka-śāstra* (one fascicle). These two aforementioned treatises.
These were translated at Jinhuasi Temple, totaling fourteen works comprising eighty-five fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
there was the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci from the city of Vārāṇasī in South India, who served under the Eastern Wei.
The Wei name is Zhixi.
From the beginning of the Yuangxiang era until the end of the Xinghe era,
he translated [this work] at the capital of Ye.
At that time, although Bodhiruci also translated scriptures on both earlier and later occasions,
the catalogs of various collections were transmitted and transcribed [as distinct works].
The titles *Qushang púti* (Going Above Bodhi) and *Pànruò zì* (Syllables of Prajñā) are attributed solely to the translation of Liu Zhi;
it is unknown which Liu Zhi this refers to.
To this day, various catalogs have been cross-referenced and compared.
This work contains erroneous passages and overlapping sections that are difficult to verify and establish definitively.
I hope that future scholars of broad learning will investigate it.
February. *Bhavaśuṇa-saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, four fascicles. Translated in the first year of the Yuánxiàng era.

From the residence of Minister Gongsun Sheng were obtained three fascicles of the Mahākāśyapa Sūtra and one fascicle of the Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja-rāja-praśna-buddha-pūjā Sūtra; these two aforementioned sūtras.
These were produced together in the third year of the Xinghe era, totaling eight fascicles from the Right Three Departments.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
the Prince of Ujjayinī in Central India, named Upaśūna, arrived from the East Wei.
Translated at Ye City by Weiyang (Gao Kong);
Sengfang recorded it in writing.
3. *Loyang Qielan Ji* (Records of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang) by Yang Xuanzhi, in five fascicles, or sometimes bound as one large volume.
This work, consisting of five fascicles, was compiled by Yang Xuanzhi, the Governor of Qicheng Commandery.
The preface states:
"The records of the Three Mounds and Five Canons;
the words of the Nine Schools and the Hundred Masters."
Furthermore, while principles reside within the human realm, their significance does not extend beyond it.
As for the source of the One Vehicle and the Two Truths, and the purport of the six supernatural powers and threefold penetration,
these are fully detailed in the Western Regions but have not been recorded in the Eastern Land.
Recently, I have been moved by dreams in which a full moon radiates its light;
at dawn, the gates are adorned with images of the white-eyebrowed one,
and at night, high above, the form of the dark-blue-haired one is depicted.
From that time on, the vogue of vying for status spread ever wider.
By the time of the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, there were only forty-two monasteries remaining.
When the Imperial Wei dynasty received the Mandate and took possession of Mount Song and the Luo River, [the number increased].
Their sincere faith increased ever more profusely, and the propagation of the Dharma flourished beyond measure.
Kings, princes, and high officials discarded their elephants and horses as if casting off a pair of sandals.
Ordinary officials and wealthy families relinquished their wealth and resources as if discarding mere footprints; consequently,
monasteries stood side by side like the teeth of a comb, and jeweled stupas were arrayed in dense clusters.
They vie with one another to capture the celestial countenance;
they compete to transcribe the shadows within the mountains.
The golden spires rival the Cloud Terrace in height.
The lecture hall was as magnificent as the Apang Palace;
how could it have been merely wood clothed in brocade and embroidery, or earth draped in vermilion and purple?
When the many hardships of the Yongxi era arrived and the imperial carriage moved to Ye, [the temple followed].
The monks and nuns of various monasteries were also relocated from time to time.
In the first year of the Wuding era,
I happened to travel on official business and once again visited Luoyang.
The walls and buildings were collapsing and ruined, with thorn bushes forming a forest;
wild beasts made their dens upon the desolate steps,
and mountain birds gathered in the courtyard trees.
Playing children and cowherds loitered upon the nine thoroughfares;
farmers grew old in their fields.
As millet is planted before the twin towers,
one first realizes that the sentiment of "the sprouting wheat" is not confined to the ruins of Yin;
the sorrow of "millet growing wild" truly applies to the House of Zhou as well.
Within and without the capital city, there were formerly more than one thousand monasteries;
today, they are desolate and the sound of bells is rarely heard.
I fear that in future generations, nothing will remain to be passed down.
Therefore, I have compiled this record.
However, as the number of temples is vast, it is impossible to transcribe them all;
what is recorded here consists only of the great monasteries.
Among these, the minor ones derive from auspicious anomalies and worldly conventional matters;
first beginning with the interior of the city,
they subsequently extend to the exterior.
The titles of the sections are listed here to record their distances;
there are five chapters in total.
My talent is not suited for commentary or composition, and thus many omissions remain.
Later gentlemen should examine its omissions in detail. 4.
*Li Kuò’s Catalogue of the Various Scriptures*, one fascicle. The above is one catalogue, one fascicle, from the era of Emperor Wu of the Liáng dynasty.
Li Kuo, a lay follower of pure faith from Luoyang,
was commissioned by imperial edict during the Yongping era of the Wei dynasty to compile this work.
Kuo was well-versed in both Buddhist and secular studies, and his commentaries and catalogues of the scriptures were highly systematic and well-ordered.

6. One fascicle of the *Mahābhūta-śāstra-triṃśikā* by Narendrayaśas of the Northern Qi dynasty; recorded in the Tang Neidian lu. Fourteen fascicles of the *Bodhisattva-jian-shi-san-mei-jing* (Bodhisattva Jñānasamādhi Sūtra) of the Northern Qi, translated in the fourth year of the Tiangong era.
In the second year of the Tiānshǒng era, twelve fascicles of the *Candragarbha-sūtra* were produced at Tiānpíng Temple.
In the eighth year of the Tiānbão era, eleven fascicles of the *Samādhirāja-sūtra* (Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra) were produced at Tiānpíng Temple.
In the ninth year of Tenpō, he produced the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* in five fascicles at Tientian Temple.
He also produced the *Sumerugarbha-sūtra* in two fascicles and the *Ratnolkā-sūtra*—also known as the *Dīpadāna-puṇya-sūtra*—in one fascicle, likewise at Tientian Temple.
The two aforementioned sutras, along with the seven-fascicle *Dharmatrāta-abhidharma-śāstra*,
were translated at Tiantian Temple in the ninth year of the Tenpō era;
and the seven works totaling fifty-two fascicles were translated at Tiantian Temple in the second year of the Heqing era during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Northern Zhou.
Translated at Ye City by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas, a śramaṇa and head of the monastic community from the kingdom of Udyāna in North India during the Gao Qi dynasty;
"Narendrayaśas" means "Honored Renown" in the Qi language.
Dharmajñāna, the eldest son of the Śramaṇa-superintendent Guptabhadra (Gautama Prajñāruci),
whose name means "Dharma-wisdom" in the Qi language,
acted as the interpreter.

One fascicle of the *Dvāviṃśatisāhasrasarvatathāgataguhyamudrānirdeśa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Sarvatathāgata-guhyamudrā), also known as the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. Thus, this one sūtra consists of one fascicle.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou,
the lay practitioner Wan-mei Yi of the Gao Qi dynasty translated [this work] in the city of Ye.
Yi’s original surname was the Xianbei clan name Wan-mei.
He left home at a young age to serve as a disciple of a Brahmin;
he was exceptionally intelligent and wise, proficient in Sanskrit script and language, and skilled in incantations and medical arts.
Consequently, he was included among the translators.
7. The Chen family [collection]: 1. *Kunāradatta-buddha-abhidharma-sūtra*, nine fascicles; 2. *Anuttara-āśraya-sūtra*, two fascicles. Translated in the second year of the Yongding era.
At Jingtu Monastery in Nankang, he produced one fascicle of the *Jiejing* (Sūtra on the Analysis of the Sections). This sūtra originally consisted of eighteen chapters;
this current single fascicle contains only the fourth chapter.
This is a brief excerpt from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (True Meaning) for the purpose of verifying the meaning; it is the third translation.
It differs from those produced during the Qin dynasty by Kumārajīva and during the Wei dynasty by Bodhiruci.

These are identical in substance to the original texts, differing only in their degree of detail. *Guangyi famen jing* (Sūtra on the Extensive Meaning of the Dharma Gate), one fascicle; *Sengshidu lü* (Vinaya of Saṃgharakṣita), one fascicle; *Chenyu zongshe xiuchanding fa* (Cantonese Title: Compendium of Methods for Cultivating Dhyāna and Samādhi), one fascicle; *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-vyākhyā*, twenty-one fascicles; *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-mūla*, sixteen fascicles; *Lishi apitan* (Lokasthāna-abhidharma), ten fascicles—translated in the third year of the Yongding era; *She dacheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra), fifteen fascicles—translated in the fourth year of the Tianjia era.

At Zhizhi Temple in Guangzhou, it was produced with Huikai serving as the scribe: the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* in twelve fascicles (or four fascicles), the *Catuḥsatya-śāstra* in four fascicles, the *Saṃgha-śāstra* in three fascicles, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* in three fascicles, which is the second translation.
