The *Upāsaka-pañcaśīla-saṃkṣepa-śāstra* (A Brief Treatise on the Five Precepts for Lay Followers), one fascicle, was produced at Qihuan Temple in the eighth year of the Yuanjia era. It is also titled the *Five Precepts Characteristics*.
This work appears in the *Gaoseng zhuan bielu*, the *Baocang lu*, and other catalogs.
It is also called the *Brief Treatise on the Five Precepts*.

According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and the *Catalogue of Chanting* (*Changlu*), there is a work titled *The Twenty-two Precepts for the Faithful*, which is also called the *Twenty-two Precepts for the Full Practice of Laymen and Laywomen Free from Desire*.
Also titled *The Three Refuges and Upāsaka Precepts*.

*A Record of the Demeanor of Śrāmaṇeras* (one fascicle), recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. *A Record of the Distinction between Sūtras and Vinaya* (one fascicle). The above seven works comprise thirty-eight fascicles in total.
The Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of Kaśmīra—
Guṇavarman meaning "Armor of Merit" in the Song language—
arrived at Jianye during the Yuanjia era.
Emperor Wen received him in audience and inquired after his well-being with great earnestness.
The Emperor then remarked, "I,
your disciple, have long desired to observe the fasts and refrain from killing."
I have been compelled to sacrifice my life for the sake of material things and have failed to follow my own aspirations.
Now that the Dharma Master has traveled from no less than ten thousand li to transform this land,
what teachings will you impart to us?
Guṇavarman said:
"The Way resides in the mind and not in external affairs;
the Dharma arises from oneself and not from others."
Furthermore, the cultivation practiced by emperors and kings differs from that of commoners.
A commoner is of humble station and inferior reputation; his words lack authority.
If he does not discipline himself and subject his person to hardship, what purpose will his practice serve?
The Emperor takes the four seas as his home and the myriad people as his children.
When he utters a single virtuous word, both men and women rejoice;
when he implements a single benevolent policy, both humans and spirits are brought into harmony.
When punishments do not cause untimely deaths and labor does not exhaust the people's strength,
it will cause wind and rain to arrive at their proper times and cold and warmth to correspond with the seasons.
The hundred grains flourish profusely, and the mulberry and hemp grow luxuriantly.
Thus, the observance of the fast is truly great,
and the abstention from killing is likewise manifold.
"Would it not be more truly a great act of salvation to sacrifice half a day's meal in order to save the life of a single bird?
The Emperor then leaned on his desk and sighed, saying,
"Ordinary people are deluded regarding profound principles."
Śramaṇas who stagnate in proximate teachings and are deluded regarding distant principles claim that the ultimate Way is but empty talk.
Those who stagnate in proximate teachings are then fettered by the literal words of the texts.
As for what Dharma Master Guṇavarman said, it was truly enlightening and profoundly insightful;
he was one with whom one could discuss the boundaries between the celestial and the human.
Consequently, an imperial decree was issued for him to reside at Jetavana Monastery, where his provisions were provided most generously.
While he was constantly engaged in translating the aforementioned sutras, śāstras,
and records during the summer retreat at Dinglin Temple,
there was a believer who gathered flowers and spread them over his seat.
Only the lotus upon which Māra sat was even more brilliantly colored;
the assembly was all struck with wonder and amazement.
Later, he returned to the Jetavana and suddenly passed away.
Before his death, he composed a testamentary document consisting of thirty-six lines of verse,
in which he personally declared that he had realized the second fruit of the path.
He entrusted this to his disciple Āśāla, saying:
"After my passing, you may show this text to both the monks of India and the people of this land.
Furthermore, at the time of his death, his disciples all saw an object shaped like a dragon.
It was about one *chi* in length and hung straight up in the air beside the corpse.
Its remaining verse said:
First, I pay homage to the Triple Gem and to the venerable elders of pure precepts.
In this turbid age, there is much flattery and crookedness.
Deceitful and lacking sincerity, foolish and deluded,
they do not recognize the truth;
harboring envy, they look down upon those with virtue.
For this reason, the various worthy sages conceal their traces in the world;
I, Guṇavarman, am one such.
The time has come for my life's activities to end;
the wholesome merits I have acquired,
I shall now describe as they truly are.
Not with a crooked or deceitful mind,
nor out of hope for fame or profit,
but in order to exhort the indolent masses.
It increases all Buddha-dharmas;
such is the power of the Great Dharma.
O virtuous ones, listen all with close attention.
In the past, amidst the wilderness,
I first observed a corpse:
bloated, infested with worms, and decaying.
Foul-smelling, putrid, and flowing with blood—
fix the mind upon that place:
such is the nature of this body.
Constantly perceiving the marks of this body,
the moth of craving has no fear of the fire;
thus it is of immeasurable kinds.
Practice the meditation on a corpse,
relinquish other forms of learned wisdom,
and take refuge among the trees of the forest.
That night he applied himself with single-minded diligence;
his right contemplation was never forgotten,
and the objective realm remained constantly before him.
Just as one looks into a clear mirror, so too am I;
through this, the mind becomes tranquil and still.
The body becomes exceedingly bright and pure;
the coolness therein is itself bliss,
increasing great joy.
Then, a mind free from attachment arises;
it transforms into the appearance of a skeleton,
and the white bones manifest before one.
The joints decay and fall apart;
the white bones are completely worn away.
Untainted wisdom blazes forth.
Having subdued thoughts and contemplated the characteristics of phenomena,
I then attained such a state:
my body was peaceful and exceedingly supple.
Through such skillful means of cultivation,
one progresses and further increases;
even the most minute particles perish moment by moment.
When the mindfulness of the body is established through the discoloration [of robes],
this is the perfection of the body.
For what reason would desire arise?
Knowing that these arise from various delusions,
like a fish greedy for a hook and bait,
they— and immeasurable others— are ruined.
Contemplating moment by moment its decay and dissolution,
one knows that its basis arises from the monkey-like mind.
Karma and the fruits of karmic retribution perish moment by moment according to conditions;
these various things are known by the mind.
This is the non-differentiation of dharmic characteristics;
it is the mindfulness of wisdom born of reflection,
which is fulfilled through successive stages of cultivation.
Observing the various characteristics of phenomena,
his mind became increasingly clear and lucid.
Within that state of intense radiance, I—
Clearly seeing the four foundations of mindfulness,
one practices with faith in the objective sphere;
gathering the mind, one dwells focused upon that object.
Suffering is like a blazing sword;
it arises from the turning of craving.
When craving is exhausted, it is like nirvana.
He sees throughout those three realms beings whose bodies are utterly emaciated, scorched by the flames of death,
yet who take delight in their own skillful means.
The body gradually becomes fully restored,
and the marks of supreme excellence arise;
the same applies to the stages of *mūrdhan* and *kṣānti*.
This arises within my mind as the true and correct application of skillful means;
gradually, it narrows its objective field.
The joy of tranquil extinction increases;
one attains the supreme mundane dharma,
contemplating the ultimate truth in a single thought-moment.
The sequential arising of the patience of the Dharma is called the untainted path;
it [severs] false appearances and all objective realms.
Completely transcending all names and designations,
one realizes the meaning of the ultimate truth;
thereby eliminating afflictions and attaining refreshing clarity.
Accomplishing the fruit of samādhi,
it is a stainless and cooling condition;
neither surging nor sinking.
Wisdom is pure like the morning sun;
serene and perfectly abiding,
it is the singular mark of quiescence.
This was not proclaimed by me;
only a Buddha can realize and know it.
This is the *Nāpābhidharma*.
The five causes and conditions of the fruit have been explained;
one who knows the true meaning practices accordingly,
such that even names cannot perceive it.
Explanations and treatises differ in their various branches,
yet the principle of practice is non-dual;
it is only through partial attachment that there is right and wrong.
The realized one has no conflict;
they cultivate all manner of wondrous signs.
For now, I shall not proclaim them.
Fearing that people would give rise to false conceptions and delude the world,
[the Buddha] taught the characteristics of the marks of merit for cultivation therein.
I have explained only a small portion;
if one understands well,
one will understand this dependent origination.
In the borders of the kingdom of Mālava,
he first attained the initial fruit of sainthood at a mountain monastery in an araṇya.
He withdrew from the world to practice in seclusion.
Later, in the kingdom of Siṃhala,
in a village named Kapila, he resided.
Through further cultivation, one attains the second fruit;
this is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
From this point on, there are many obstacles.
Obstructing the path to cultivation and the departure from desire,
they see me practicing seclusion;
they know this place to be empty and quiet.
All gave rise to a sense of rare wonder,
and offerings and gains vied with one another to arrive;
I regard them as fire and poison.
A great sense of weary detachment arose in his heart;
he fled the turmoil and drifted upon the sea to Java and Lâm-yìp.
Driven by the winds of karmic action,
he followed the conditions that led him to the borders of Song;
thus, among these various kingdoms, he arrived.
Establishing the Buddha-dharma according to one's capacity,
without questioning what ought to be questioned,
one contemplates with truth, reality, and genuine insight.
Now this body is extinguished;
it is as silent as a lamp going out. 7.
*Saṃghavarman’s Saṃyuktābhidharmavibhāṣā*, fourteen fascicles, translated for a second time at Changgan Monastery in the tenth year of the Yuanjia era.
This is largely identical to the previous version with minor differences. It is the *Mātṛkā-vinaya* in ten fascicles; it is also called the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
It was translated at Pínglè Monastery in Mólíng during the twelfth year of the Yuánjiā era.

The *Jian Daohui* (Record of Wisdom on Seeing the Path), the *Dayong Pusa Fenbie Yebao Ji* (Collection of the Bodhisattva Dayong’s Analysis of Karmic Retribution) in one fascicle, the *Longshu Pusa Quanfa Zhuwang Yaojie* (Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna’s Essential Verses Exhorting Kings) in one fascicle, and the *Qing Shengseng Yu Wen* (Text for Inviting the Holy Sangha to Bathe) in one fascicle are all found in the *Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) and the *Bielu* (Separate Records). These five works comprise twenty-seven fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor Wen,
there was the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman from India;
"Saṃghavarman" means "Armour of the Multitude" in the Song language.
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era, he arrived from Jianye.
He was proficient in the Vinaya-piṭaka and the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
Liu Yikang, the Prince of Pengcheng, revered his model of monastic discipline.
Please accept him as your teacher;
his reputation was preeminent within the monasteries of the capital.
Hui-guan observed that Guṇavarman had a profound understanding of the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and could recite it with complete fluency.
Although the Tripitaka Master and others had previously translated it,
they had not yet managed to transcribe it; therefore,
he requested that it be translated once more.
Baoyun transmitted the words,
and Guan himself took dictation;
after one full cycle, it was completed.
Thereafter, the *Mātṛkā* and other texts were successively produced. 8.
The *Saṃyuktāgama* in fifty fascicles, translated by Guṇabhadra at Waguan Temple.
Faxian brought this from abroad.

Daohui saw it in the Song-Qi Records of Various Matters. The *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* in twelve fascicles was translated together with Buddhabhadra and Bodhiyaśas. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* in four fascicles [was translated] in the twentieth year of the Yuanjia era.
Translated at Daochang Monastery;
Huiguan received the dictation.
It appears in the catalogs of Daohui, Sengyou, Fashang, and others. The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* in four fascicles was also produced at Daochang Monastery.

The *Past and Present Causes and Effects Sūtra* (Guoqu xianzai yinguo jing) in four fascicles—recorded in the *Jian Daohui*, *Song Qi*, and *Sengyou Fashang Bie Lu*—was translated at Xin Temple in Jingzhou;
this is the third edition.

It is largely identical to the versions translated by Zhu Dalü of the Han dynasty and [An] Xuan of the Wu dynasty, such as the *Benqi jing* and the *Ruixiang yingyan jing*, though the wording differs slightly; it appears in the catalogs of Shixing, Sengyou, Li Kuò, and others. The *Shi liu shier jian jing* (Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views) in four fascicles appears in separate records; Sengyou’s catalog states it consists of one fascicle. The *Dafangguang baoqie jing* (Sūtra of the Great Vaipulya Precious Casket) in three fascicles appears in Li Kuò’s record. The *Xiànzài fó míng jīng* (Sūtra of the Names of Buddhas Present) in three fascicles was [translated] on the seventh day of the first month in the twenty-ninth year of the Yuánjiā era.
It was translated at Jingzhou by Liu Yixuan, Prince of Nanqiao.
It is also titled *The Names of the Buddhas Presently Manifesting Their Splendor*.

This is recorded in the *Shixing lu* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. There is also the three-fascicle *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Skillful Means and Supernatural Transformations*, recorded in the *Li Kuò lu*, and the three-fascicle *Jìngdù sānmèi jīng*.

In the *Juanjian* (Record of Scrolls), it is noted that Li Kuoluo’s catalogue records two fascicles of the *Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning of Continuous Liberation*, translated at Dong’an Temple; this is also found in the catalogues of Daohui, Sengyou, Li Kuoluo, Fashang, and others.
It is recorded that two fascicles of the *Mahābherī-haraka-sūtra* were translated at Dong’an Temple, as seen in the catalogues of Daohui, Sengyou, Li Kuoluo, and other separate records.

Two fascicles of the *Āraṇyaka-dhyāna-śikṣā-sūtra* are found in Li Kuoluo’s record. One fascicle of the *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahopāya-sūtra* was translated in Danyang Commandery; Baoyun acted as the oral interpreter and Huiquan served as the scribe.
*Shou jian dao hui* (Receiving the Wisdom of the Path of Seeing), one fascicle; recorded in the *Song Qi Lu*, translated during the Xiaojian era by Yu and Kuo. This is the eighth translation.

Regarding the *Shou jian dao hui*, the *Song Qi Lu* states it is largely identical to the versions produced by Kang Sengkai, Zhi Qian, Bo Yan, Zhu Fahu, Kumārajīva, Zhu Fali, Baoyun, and others, though they differ in length and phrasing.

*Bing tou lu tu luo sha wei you ta yan wang shuo fa jing* (The Scripture on Piṇḍola Bharadvāja Preaching the Dharma for King Udayana), one fascicle. *Ban ni yuan jing* (The Nirvāṇa Sūtra), one fascicle. Translated at Xin Temple in the first year of the Xiaojian era. This is the [ninth]... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
The second translation either lacks the character "ban" (般) or is largely identical with slight variations to the two-fascicle *Nirvāṇa* translated by Zhu Fahu of the Jin dynasty;

it is recorded in Daohui’s *Song Qi Lu* that this was translated for Sima Yu, the Prince of Nanqiao and Minister of Works, at Jingzhou in the twenty-ninth year of the Yuanjia era. This second version differs slightly from the one translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty, as noted in the records of Sengyou and Baochang.
There is also the one-fascicle *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra*, translated at Xin Temple in Jingzhou, as recorded in the *Wu Lu*. Furthermore, there is the *Ananta-dhāraṇī-mukha-sūtra*.
*Jian wu lu san xiao jie jing* (One fascicle), seen in the *Bie lu*. *Mou lien jiang long wang jing* (One fascicle). *A nan jian ji yue ti ku wu chang jing* (One fascicle).

*Chu za a han sheli fu deng bi qiu de shen zuo zheng jing* (One fascicle). *Fo wang wei jie she bing jing* (One fascicle). *Qing ban te bi qiu jing* (One fascicle); also known as *Shi fo ming a nan yi zui sheng chang zhe jing* (One fascicle). *Mou lien di bo shu wang ji bao jing* (One fascicle). *Sheli fu ban ni yuan jing* (One fascicle). *Chu sheng jing mo he jie she du pin mu jing* (One fascicle). *A na liu qi nian zhang jing* (One fascicle).
*Za zang jing* (One fascicle). *Xu kong zang pusa jing* (One fascicle). *Pusa he yu jing* (One fascicle). The second edition.
The *Amitābha Sūtra*, one fascicle; the *Sūtra on the Non-Activity of All Dharmas*, one fascicle;

the *Sūtra of the Poor Son Sudrāṣṭra*, one fascicle; the *Sūtra on Saving an Entire Country by Killing a Dragon*, one fascicle (found in Li Kuò’s catalog); the *Sūtra of the Immeasurable Meanings* [extracted] from the *Collection on the Six Pāramitās*, one fascicle (found in Li Kuò’s catalog);

the *Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of Holding Boundless Limits*, one fascicle; the *Sūtra on the Pearl Falling into the Sea*, one fascicle; and the *Sūtra on the Emergence of the Future Selection of the Evil Age*, one fascicle.

*Jie jing* (Dhātu-sūtra), one fascicle; *Ānandamukha-nihārita-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Fo rù gànlù tiáozhèngyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Buddha Entering the Ambrosia to Rectify and Harmonize the Mind), one fascicle; *Chū dà shíèrmén jīng* (Sūtra of the Emergence of the Great Twelve Gates), one fascicle; *Guòqù xíng dānpōluómì jīng* (Sūtra on the Past Practice of the Dānapāramitā), one fascicle;

*Bǎnxíng liù pōluómì jīng* (Sūtra on the Original Practices of the Six Pāramitās), one fascicle. The above titles, which are not annotated in various catalogs, are all found in the first volume of the *Bié lù* (Separate Catalog).

*Yú dìyì wǔxiàng lüèjí* (Brief Collection of the Five Characteristics of the Ultimate Truth), one fascicle, translated at Dong’an Temple; seen in the *Sēngyòu lù*. *Ènzàng fǎshī zìshù yù* (Metaphor Self-Described by Master Ènzàng), one fascicle; seen in [the same].
Miscellaneous Records: The seventy-eight scriptures listed above comprise one hundred and sixty-one fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen, the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra from the kingdom of Central India [translated them].
In the Song language, his name was Guṇabhadra.
He was well-versed in Mahāyāna studies;
his contemporaries also referred to him as Mahāyāna.
He was also called Yan.
In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at the capital of Yangdu,
where the Emperor held him in profound reverence and esteem.
Prince Liu Yikang of Pengcheng and Prince Liu Yixuan of Nanqiao both served him as their teacher.
By imperial decree, he was stationed at Qihuan Monastery.
He further requested that the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and other texts be translated;
Baoyun acted as the oral interpreter,
and Huiguan served as the scribe.
Later, he followed Prince Xiao in his pacification of Jingzhou.
There, at Xin Temple, he again brought forth the *Anuttara-rāja-sūtra* and other scriptures.
In total, the translations produced by him before and after amounted to more than one hundred fascicles.
Mostly, his disciple Fayong acted as his interpreter.
Once, Prince Qiao invited him to lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
Guṇabhadra reflected that he was not yet proficient in the Song language and felt ashamed and sighing within his heart.
Thereupon, she focused her mind exclusively on performing prostrations and repentance day and night,
invoking Avalokiteśvara and praying for a response from the unseen realm.
Consequently, she dreamed of a person dressed in white garments, holding a sword and carrying a human head, who came before her and said:
"Why are you grieving?
Dhāyī prostrated himself with his forehead to the ground and explained his thoughts in detail.
The man replied:
Without much anxiety,
he immediately exchanged his head for that of the *ḍomba*, fixed the new head in place,
and after commanding him to turn around, he asked:
"Have you attained freedom from pain?
Da replied, "I am no longer in pain.
Suddenly, he felt his mind and spirit awaken with joy.
At dawn he arose, fully grasping the meaning of the Song dynasty’s discourse;
thereupon he proceeded to lecture and debate on the commentaries with a fluency like a flowing stream.
Later, he returned to Yangdu.
During an imperial banquet where the princes and dukes had all assembled, the Emperor summoned Guṇabhadra.
Before he had yet shaved his hair, the master’s head was already white and radiant.
Seeing him from afar, the Emperor turned to the Minister of the Interior, Xie Zhuang, and said:
The Master Mahāyāna is intelligent and possesses keen understanding;
however, as his old age approaches,
I have tested him with these questions.
His demeanor must surely have been able to perceive the Emperor's thoughts.
As Guṇabhadra ascended the steps,
the Emperor went out to meet him and said to him:
"Today, Master of the Mahāyāna has not failed the purpose of our journey from afar.
Beyond this, how can there be anything else? There is only the Mahāyāna.
The Master immediately replied in kind:
This poor monk, admiring your transformative teachings, traveled from afar to return to the imperial capital.
Having received your patronage for nearly thirty years,
I am deeply humbled by the Emperor’s gracious favor.
"But now, I am a man of seventy, old and infirm;
I have no further time remaining, for death alone awaits me.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and marveled at his quick-witted eloquence.
The Emperor issued an edict for Tuo Jin to approach the imperial banquet and take his seat;
the entire court turned their eyes toward him, honoring and admiring him.
Furthermore, he was skilled in the arts of incantation.
The details are contained in the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*),
so they are not recorded here in full.
The *Biographies of Faying* (*Fayong lu*) merely states:
The Venerable translated seventy-three fascicles of sutras;
it is known that he did not exhaust [the entire canon].
Now, consulting various catalogs, I have listed them all in their entirety.

9. *Dharmamitra-canyābhiṣmaya-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna by Dharmamitra), three fascicles; also called *Canyā-dharmābhiṣmaya*. Translated at Qihuan Temple in the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era. Recorded in the catalogues of Sengyou and Fashang. *Wumen-canying-yao-yong-fa* (The Essential Methods for the Five-Gate Dhyāna Sutra), one fascicle. Recorded in the catalogues of Sengyou and Fashang. *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (Sutra on the Method of Contemplating the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra), one fascicle. Extracted from the *Gambhīra-guṇa-sūtra*; also called the *Samantabhadra-visualization Sutra*.
The *Jianyou lu* records one fascicle of the *Xukongzang guan jing*, also titled *Guankongzang pusa jing*,
and also simply called *Xukongzang pusa jing*.

The *Jian Daohui* (Catalogue of the Sui, Qi, and Sengyou), as well as the records of Li Kuò, list the following six scriptures: 1. *Zhufa yongwang jing* (Sūtra of the King Valiant in All Dharmas), one fascicle; 2. *Fo sheng daoli tian wei mu shuofa jing* (Sūtra of the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother), one fascicle; 3. *Zhuan nushen jing* (Sūtra on Transforming the Female Body), one fascicle; 4. *Xiangyi jing* (Elephant-Arm Sūtra), one fascicle; 5. *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Questions of the Householder Ugra), one fascicle; 6. *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-vidyā-mantra-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Divine Incantation of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha), one fascicle. These are the aforementioned six scriptures.
I have also consulted Li Kuò’s *Wei Shi Lu* (Record of the Wei Dynasty), which comprises ten sections and twelve fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen,
the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra, Dhammarakṣa (Tánmómìduō), [was active].
In the Song language, his name was Fashou.
He was born with joined eyebrows.
By nature he was profound and possessed great wisdom and discernment.
There were always benevolent deities who protected him in secret, concealing their forms.
Whenever he approached the borders of a kingdom, these deities would invariably manifest in dreams to inform the king;
likewise, they did the same when he was known to be departing.
He vowed that his life's purpose would be to travel abroad to teach and transform others.
By nature he was pure and austere, unconcerned with fame or profit.
Upon first arriving in Dunhuang, he immediately established a meditation hall on a secluded and open site.
He planted one thousand persimmon trees and established a garden of one hundred mu.
The assembly of practitioners gathered in great numbers, arriving like clouds.
At the beginning of the Yuanjia era, he came to Jianye and settled at Zhongsi Temple.
In the evening, he rested at the Jetavana Monastery,
where he immediately translated the *Dhyāna Sūtras* and various divine incantations (*mantra*),
while also transmitting the painted images of the Kapiśa spirit king.
Up to the present day, this remains the standard method.

*The Scripture on the Contemplation of the Two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Contemplation of Amitāyus*, one fascicle. The above two works comprise two fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor Wen,
there was a śramaṇa from the Western Regions named Gītamitra,
which in the language of Song means "Renowned in His Time."
By nature upright and with few desires,
he was proficient in the Tripiṭaka and possessed extensive knowledge.
He was particularly skilled in meditative contemplation.
At the beginning of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at the capital,
where the Emperor held him in high esteem and bestowed great praise upon him.
By Imperial Decree, he was appointed to reside at Daolin Monastery on Mount Zhong; [the Emperor] commanded that these two sutras above be constantly received,
upheld, recited, and chanted, for they are the secret arts for transforming obstacles and the great causes for attaining the Pure Land.
Therefore, the śramaṇa Senghan prayed for its translation;
Senghan personally transcribed it by hand.
This is recorded in both the *Daohui’s Song-Qi Records* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
11. *Dharmodgata-avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle; the second translation.

Slightly different from the version translated by Zhu Fahu during the Jin dynasty. The *Foguo zhuan* (Account of the Buddhist Kingdoms) in five fascicles, in which Dharmodgata himself recounts his travels to the Western Regions. The above two works comprise six fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor Wu,
in the first year of the Yongchu era (420 CE), the śramaṇa Dharmodgata— translated into Chinese as Fayong— from the country of Huanglong arrived [in China].
He gathered twenty-five fellow practitioners, including the monk Shi Sengmeng,

Regarding the *Bodhisattva Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection) in six fascicles—sometimes simply called the *Nianfo Sanmei Jing*: ... [text continues] ... It is said that in the past, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a bhikṣu who practiced the samādhi of Buddha-recollection. He constantly sat in meditation, reciting the Buddha’s name. At that time, there was a king who heard of this and, wishing to test him, disguised himself as a commoner and went to the bhikṣu’s dwelling. He asked, "What are you doing? The bhikṣu replied, "I am practicing the samādhi of Buddha-recollection. The man asked, "What benefit does this bring? The bhikṣu answered, "One will attain rebirth in the Pure Land and never again fall into the three evil realms. The man then said, "If that is so, I shall now go to the Buddha and ask him about this. Having said this, he departed. Later, the king went to the Buddha and related his encounter. The Buddha told the king, "That bhikṣu is a person of great merit. He has already attained the stage of non-retrogression. If one recites the Buddha’s name with a single-minded heart, one will surely be born in the Western Land. This is not empty talk.

The king, having heard this, believed and accepted it, and thereafter he and his ministers all took up the practice of Buddha-recollection. Because of this, they were all born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss after their deaths. Therefore, the sutra says: "If one recites the Buddha’s name with a focused mind, one will immediately see the Buddha and be born in the Pure Land. Thus, the power of Buddha-recollection is inconceivable and its benefits are immeasurable. One should diligently cultivate this practice without negligence. [End of excerpt] The above is a summary of the content found in the *Nianfo Sanmei Jing*. It emphasizes the efficacy of the practice of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*) as a means for attaining rebirth in the Pure Land. The text serves as a scriptural authority for the Pure Land tradition, illustrating through narrative how the sincere invocation of the Buddha's name leads to liberation from the cycle of birth and death.

In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, the Imperial Scribe for Translating Scriptures, Your Servant Fei Changfang, submitted this "Record of the Reigns of the Emperors of the Qi, Liang, and Zhou Dynasties.
This was compiled in succession by those who presided over the transmission of the Chan teachings.
Xiao Daocheng [is the first].
A native of Linyi.
Having received the abdication from the Song dynasty,
he styled his reign Qi and continued to have its capital at Jiankang.
During the Jianyuan era, a wild fire broke out in Ancheng, consuming the entire marsh until nothing remained but ashes;
yet, in a single patch of ground measuring only several zhang, the grass alone did not burn.
Upon going to examine its center, they discovered a golden image.
As auspicious omens were thus manifested and the sacred transformation was restored,
the Minister Jingling Wenzhuan Wang Ziliang directed his aspirations toward the stream of the Dharma and extensively propagated its teachings.
The succession was transmitted through seven rulers for twenty-three years before they yielded the throne to Xiao Yan of the Liang dynasty.
A native of Lanling, Xiao Yan received the abdication from Qi.
He also resided in Jiankang.
Once the Emperor had ascended the throne,
he contemplated [bringing peace] to all living beings.
Equaling the stage of Perfect Enlightenment and meeting together with the Omniscient One,
he presides over the court with effortless ease, extensively propagating the teachings of the sutras.
He extensively researched ancient lore and widely collected surviving texts;
by fanning the pure winds of civilization, he benefited both the Buddhist community and the secular world.
This continued until the seventh year of the Tianjian era.
He considered that as the True Dharma, Semblance Dharma, and Final Dharma successively declined, faith and devotion were increasingly waning;
furthermore, the Tripitaka was so vast and extensive that few were able to master it comprehensively.
He therefore commanded the śramaṇas Sengmin and Baochang and others [to undertake this task].
The essential matters of the Sūtras and Vinaya were recorded and arranged according to their categories;
this work is titled *Jīnglǜ yìxiàng* (Diverse Phenomena of the Sūtras and Vinaya) and consists of fifty fascicles in total.
In the fourteenth year,
he further issued an edict to the śramaṇa Sengshao to compile the *Catalogue of the Scriptures in the Hualin Buddha Hall* in four fascicles.
As [the Emperor] was still not fully informed,
in the seventeenth year,
he again issued an edict to the śramaṇa Baochang.
He further compiled a four-fascicle catalog of scriptures,
which clearly distinguished between those with and without translations, as well as authentic and spurious sutras;
it comprised seventeen sections and was quite detailed.
The three rulers reigned for fifty-four years in total.
Two of these rulers had their capitals at Jiankang,
while one ruler had his capital at Jiangling.
It was extinguished by the Western Wei.
Yuwen Jue was the eldest son of Yuwen Tai, the Chancellor of the Wei Dynasty and a Xianbei from Shuozhou.
Upon Tai’s death, Jue succeeded him to the position of Chancellor.
Having received the abdication from the Western Wei, it was styled Zhou.
Its capital was at Chang'an.
It reached the reign of its third ruler, Emperor Wu (r. 560–578), whose personal name was Yong.
From the Jian-de era through the Dun-mao and up to the Zuo-e period,

all Buddhist stupas— whether built by the government or private individuals over several hundred years within the region east of Guanshan to the west— were destroyed and demolished until they were completely swept from the ground.
Rong scraped away the sacred images and burned the scriptures;
from the temples of the eight provinces,
forty thousand were removed and all granted to princes and dukes to serve as their residences.
The followers of Śākyamuni in the three regions numbered less than three million;
all were returned to military and civilian registers as common subjects.
Now that the Sun of Wisdom has set, the masses of living beings are once more shrouded in darkness.
The succession was maintained by five rulers for twenty-four years.
Beginning in the first year of the Yongchu era of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty, the year Gengshen, they received the abdication from the Eastern Jin.
It continued until the first year of the Dading era of the Zhou dynasty, the year Xinchou, when the imperial seal was offered to the Great Sui.

a total of fifty-one individuals— both Chinese and foreign, monastic and lay—
collaborated to produce translations of sūtras, vinaya, prātimokṣa-sūtras, karmavācanās, upadeśas, abhidharma-śāstras, biographies, and catalogs.

In the first year of the Wu Cheng era during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Northern Zhou dynasty,
he studied together with Yaśodhara,
following his teacher, the Tripiṭaka Master and Dhyāna Master Jayasena from the kingdom of Magadha.
Carrying the scriptures into the country,
the master and his disciples studied the local dialect together for more than twenty years.
Kumārajīva was the most excellent;
while residing in the capital and later traveling to the region of Shu,
he translated new scriptures everywhere he went.
In some instances, he supplemented previous omissions;
both the phrasing and the meaning were entirely consistent with the truth.
At that time, he encountered demonic obstacles and was pressed by the imperial authority of the sovereign.
In the third year of the Jiande era, the two teachings were suppressed.
During the summer, the sevenfold assembly of the monastic community was all compelled to adopt secular dress and a single garment.
Master Kuṃārajīva and his disciples were likewise subjected to such coercion and intimidation.
Having made no formal pledge, he cast aside his life to travel to distant lands;
undaunted by hardship and toil, he took the propagation of the Dharma as his primary mission.
Encountering the decline and extinction of the Teaching, he was thus unable to fulfill his original aspiration.
The Brahmin declined to adopt Chinese dress;
maintaining his firm resolve and integrity, he begged to return to his own country.
The state granted his request and sent him away with due ceremony.
My Zhina is truly the sea and land of Jambudvīpa;
it is where all those from distant frontiers with their diverse garments and strange forms flock together.
It is not a land of mere pleasure.
How could it be that such a state has been brought about?
Those who come seeking transformation are welcomed and accommodated;
those who long for their hometowns and wish to depart are not opposed in their leaving.
Returning northward along the route to the Turks,
he encountered the Middle-Region Tabgach Kagan,
who earnestly invited him to stay; thus, they engaged in a series of exchanges.
He said, "In the case of Zhou, there was both prosperity and decline, and the army had to toil in coming and going.
Here, there is neither ruin nor rise; you may rest at ease.
As for your provisions and offerings, they shall be made to your heart's content."
Consequently, the project was suspended for over ten years.
The Master and his fellow students all passed away before him;

only Daodu remained alone at that time. It was during the sixth year of the Wuping era of the Qi dynasty that eleven individuals—including the śramaṇas Baoxian and Daosui from Xiangzhou, as well as Zhizhou, Sengwei, Fabao, Sengtan, Zhi Zhao, and Senglü—succeeded one another in traveling westward.
He traveled back and forth for seven years,
obtaining a total of two hundred and sixty Sanskrit scriptures.
Upon his return to the Turks, he heard that the Zhou had extinguished the Qi dynasty and had simultaneously destroyed the Buddha-dharma.
If he were to retreat, it would be impossible; if he advanced, there was nowhere to turn.
As he lingered in that place, he eventually encountered one of noble character and virtue—like a thirsty man finding a drink, or one in darkness meeting with light.
They continued together to examine the newly acquired scriptures,
requesting that their titles be translated and compared with the entries in the existing catalogs;
they found them to be remarkably skillful and superior to those of previous scholars.
Xian and the others, with sincere hearts, each privately rejoiced that they had obtained the treasure and encountered the master, so that their journey was not in vain.
They made a mutual vow to burn incense and together pledged to propagate and translate [the text].
When the Great Sui dynasty received the abdication of the throne, the Buddha-dharma flourished.
Xuán and the others brought the scriptures here first to respond to this destiny,
arriving at the end of winter in the first year of the Kaiguang era.
By imperial decree, the person was assigned to the relevant office to have [the texts] translated.
It was not until the fourth year of Jue-tuo that he finally arrived in the country;

Submitted by the Academician for Translating Scriptures, Your Servant Fei Changfang, in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era. Part Two:

The Record of the Hīnayāna. Regarding the Record of the Hīnayāna: it is the Śrāvaka Piṭaka. As for the teaching that distinguishes the Buddha, it begins with his birth in the royal palace, his being supported in swaddling clothes, and his being nursed and raised.
He rode in a sheep-drawn carriage to attend school;
he was tested in the arts and crafts and entered into marriage.
At nineteen, he left the household life; at thirty, he attained the Way.
He dwelt in the world preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years.
At the age of seventy-nine,
he lay on his right side between a pair of śāla trees and entered parinirvāṇa.
In terms of the Dharma itself, it refers to the Sūtras;
alternatively, there are nine divisions or eleven divisions.
The four Āgamas, the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*,
and the Abhidharma discuss individuals such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the four fruits and four stages of approach, the five directions and seven expedients,
and those who shave their hair and beards to renounce worldly life and enter the monastic order.
The scope [of this teaching] is limited to devas and humans and does not encompass the other realms of existence.
As for afflictions, they consist of the five hindrances, the ten entanglements, and the ninety-eight proclivities.
As for the practices, they consist of the four noble truths and the twelve links of dependent origination.
One restrains the seven limbs and guards the three karmas.
The prohibitions one receives consist of the Three Refuges, the ten precepts, the two hundred and fifty, and the five hundred precepts;
these apply only for the duration of this single lifetime and do not extend to future lives.
Having merely disciplined one's own body and speech without engaging in the benefit of others,
one enters the shallow or deep waters of principle like a rabbit or a horse crossing by swimming.
Leaving the games of the city streets,
he mounted the humble vehicles of sheep and deer;
the dew that moistened him was both slight and abundant.
If one takes the roots and leaves of the middling and lesser [vehicles],
they are merely resting places for those weary and exhausted— a provisional *parinirvāṇa-city* that is not ultimate.
All such passages belong to the Hīnayāna.
Based on the four Āgamas, there arose the Sūtras, Udānavarga, *Śarīraprabheda* (The Wise and the Foolish), Avadāna (Parables), and various miscellaneous sūtras.
These consist of ten lines, five lines, one page, or half a page;
they begin with the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) and conclude with the proclamation "May it be practiced" (*dhārayatu*).
These various branches have proliferated into ten thousand scrolls;
worldly people, pursuing the superficial, mostly compete to copy fragments.
This not only wastes effort but also profoundly deviates from the original source.
However, according to the collective records and commentaries,
there are those who have emerged as separate manifestations;
for example, Avalokiteśvara appeared from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The *Sukālī-haṃsa-rāja-sūtra*, which gives rise to the mindfulness of the True Dharma,
is not included here;

only the essentials of the monastic precepts for monks and nuns from the four *vinaya* collections, along with the summaries of dignified conduct, *karmavācanā*, and miscellaneous rules, are recorded.
Since worldly people are all accustomed to [these methods], they are listed here in full.
As for those practices that are analyzed separately within this scripture,
since they are already complete in their respective sections, there is no need to duplicate them here.
The benefit derived is slight while the trouble involved is vast;
a rough calculation of what might be saved shows ten thousand sheets of paper and nearly two thousand scrolls of scripture.
The currently compiled and collected major sections and separate fascicles that are verified not to be apocryphal (liuchu) total five hundred and twenty-five works.
In total, there are one thousand seven hundred and twelve fascicles.
These have been compiled as the formal catalog for the inclusion of the Hīnayāna in the Tripiṭaka.
My own awareness is shallow and my views are narrow; in my search and reading, much has been omitted.
I hope that this may illuminate the torch of the Dharma for the sake of the wise; may we together remove the embers and add oil.

A Memorial Presenting the Kaihuang Record of the Three Jewels. Your servant Fang addresses the Throne:

Your servant has heard that those who have merited the state have their achievements recorded in the official histories, and those who have governed the people have their virtues commemorated in inscribed monuments.
How much more so for the Tathāgata, the Great Sage, whose transformative influence permeates the infinite without fail, yet who does not display his own excellence—
unlike the hundred kings whose fragrant legacy has flowed for a thousand years.
Your servant has humbly examined and perused these matters.
Since the Han and Wei dynasties, there have been translations from generation to generation;
yet the catalogs are scattered and many scriptures have lost their sources.
Rarely has anyone compiled them into a continuous whole, and at times the tradition has been interrupted.
For this reason, the Buddha entrusted the True Dharma to the kings;
thus we know that the flourishing of the Teaching depends upon the sovereign.
We humbly observe that Your Majesty has appeared in response to the destiny of the age and holds the mandate of the realm.
He received the Tathāgata’s prophecy,
succeeded to the office of a Wheel-Turning King,
and governed Jambudvīpa.
Compassionately pitying the world’s darkness, he raised the sun of wisdom;
he extensively compiled scriptures and images and grandly established monasteries,
opening wide the gate of liberation.
He guides the path for devas and humans and establishes the oars and rudders of goodness to ferry and rescue the masses;
this is truly a magnificent achievement for an era throughout the vast expanse of antiquity.
How could this humble and insignificant servant dare to venture such a reckless statement?
However, in the past when the Dharma was being suppressed, I was among those clad in dyed robes;
today, as it flourishes once more, I have returned to join the ranks of the Sangha.
Regarding contemporary events, I have had considerable opportunity to observe and hear of them.
Consequently, I shall trace the historical origins of the Buddha-dharma through its successive eras,

beginning from the year Jia-wu of King Zhuang’s reign in the Zhou dynasty when the Buddha was born in the Western Regions, until the year Ding-mao of Emperor Ming’s Yongping era in the Later Han dynasty when the scriptures were first transmitted to the East.
From that time until the present year of the Kaihuang era,
the Dingsi year, one thousand two hundred and seventy-four years have elapsed;
during this interval, auspicious omens and eminent monks have appeared in succession under successive sovereigns.
This work, titled *The Kaihuang Record of the Three Jewels*,
consists of fifteen fascicles in total.
It is intended that no aspect of the Dharma remain concealed and that the scriptures may flourish and spread.
Unable to bear my inner feelings of alarm and trepidation, I have ventured to present this memorial to report these matters for Your Majesty’s perusal.
I humbly pray that Your Heavenly Compassion will deign to bestow its divine attention upon this submission. I respectfully submit.

Preface to the General Catalogue of the Kaihuang Record of the Three Jewels On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, the Imperial Scribe for the Translation of Scriptures at Daxingshan Monastery, Your Subject Fei Changfang of Chengdu, respectfully submits this:
I humbly reflect that while the Three Jewels provide sustenance and the four modes of birth receive their nourishment, the world has witnessed periods of both flourishing and decline.
It causes people to rise or sink on their own accord:
when practiced, meritorious deeds constantly evoke rebirth in the heavens as a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) or a sovereign;
when violated, the retribution of sin is constantly endured in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as animals.
In discussing the profound benefit of aiding sentient beings, nothing surpasses the Dharma.
Why is this? The Dharma is the Mother of the Buddhas, and the Buddhas are born from the Dharma;
the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all make offerings to the Dharma.
Therefore, the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"If one makes offerings to the Dharma, one makes offerings to the Buddha.
Thus we know that the flowing current of the Dharma teachings has been transmitted through ten thousand generations.
The Buddha and the Sangha provide guidance such that benefit is simultaneous;
thus, during the rise of the Bhadrakalpa, the thousand Buddhas share the same transformative influence.
Yet, regarding the span of their lifetimes, the four sages differ in their years.
Although there are differences in the duration of their remaining in the world—
whether long or short— in terms of proclaiming and spreading the Dharma,
they are no different. There are none who do not scorch the ocean of craving to deliver sentient beings toward Nirvana.
Chiseling away at the mountains of ignorance, he guides all living beings to realize Prajñā.
Yet, Prajñā is profound and quiescent;
it is difficult to penetrate without the medium of sound.
Sound must rely upon form;
without depending on its characteristics, it has no means of manifestation.
Therefore, the realm is called the "Endurance" (Kṣānti) land.
Gathering together ten billion Mount Sumerus,
it is known in the world as Sahā;
it governs three thousand lands.
He distinguished the impure lands of the five turbidities within the three realms from the sands [of the Dharma],
and differentiated the base sheep and deer of the six paths and the two vehicles.
Out of great sage-like compassion, he descended to Kapilavastu.
The sixteen-foot golden countenance appeared within the royal palace;
the thirty-two marks shone brilliantly upon the Prince’s body.
At nineteen he left the home life, and at thirty he attained enlightenment.
For forty-nine years he dwelt in the world,
employing the skillful means of speech and sound to expound the stainless Dharma,
which he proclaimed from his own golden mouth.
A single sound is proclaimed, yet the myriad classes of beings each understand it;
since karmic conditions are not uniform, the teachings are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Ānanda’s dhāraṇī-retention leaves not a single drop lost.
It is like pouring water from one vessel into another; thus,
after entering parinirvāṇa between the twin trees,
[the teachings] were compiled at the city of Rājagṛha by Kāśyapa.
One thousand arhats examined and transcribed it in turn,
recording it upon leaves and bark and disseminating it throughout India;
five hundred [monks] from the Central Kingdom each received and upheld it.
The sixteen great kings all provided unified protection.
At the beginning of the Later Han, the era first reached Zhina (China).
Throughout the imperial dynasties, there were sixteen successive reigns.
The terminology of that region was translated into this local dialect and has been transmitted down to the present for over five hundred years.
The entries of the two ancient catalogs have been lost and fragmented.
When Master Xingdao established the school, he repaired what was deficient.
Since then, there have occasionally been differing lineages of succession;
each has recorded its own particular approach, preserving their respective perspectives.
Because the three regions were geographically remote from one another, many errors and doubts arose. Furthermore,
although translations were produced during the Qi, Zhou, and Chen dynasties,
they were not included in the official catalogs, leaving no standard for us to follow.
Furthermore, as the texts were destroyed by fire, they were entirely without basis for verification.
Fortunately, our Emperor supports the earth and upholds the heavens;
he has brought tranquility to the two polarities and cleared away all impurities throughout the six directions.
The myriad nations come to the court, and the transformation of the nine provinces is encompassed.
Diverse and ancient texts have all been gathered together.
I, your servant, am fortunate to have encountered this auspicious time.
Having the honor of participating in the translation of the scriptures and receiving the Buddha’s words,
I have not dared to forget them even during moments of leisure from my writing, whether sleeping or eating;
thus it has been for over ten years.
I consulted with the elders of former times and searched extensively before finally obtaining it;
though I have roughly compiled and stitched it together, I still fear that it may not be exhaustive.
I have conducted extensive research and wide-ranging inquiries, respectfully awaiting future scholars of talent;
for the compilation presented here,
I have briefly followed three texts as my guiding manual.
Manifesting these Three Jewels:
the auspicious signs of the Buddha’s birth followed the night-light of the Zhou dynasty,
and the propitious omens of the sutras’ transmission were received during the nocturnal dream of the Han era.
He was the primordial source and the structural pillar of the Sangha’s city walls;

Furthermore, he extensively consulted dozens of sources, including accounts of hermits, national annals, the classics, the *Sengyou ji ji*, and various dynastic histories.
Picking up those fallen feathers of the azure bird, he composed this record of its wings;
he fanned the wind of a thousand years' past for the sake of a hundred kings,

When it shines, the darkness is dispelled;

In the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era, by imperial decree, the śramaṇa Baochang compiled the *Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures), Volume One: I. Mahāyāna scriptures: 262 works in 674 fascicles. A.

Translated by multiple persons, consisting of multi-fascicle scriptures: 169 works in 467 fascicles. B. Translated by multiple persons, consisting of single-fascicle scriptures: 5 works in 19 fascicles. C.
Translated by a single person, consisting of single-fascicle scriptures: 3 [works].
Section Ninety: Ninety fascicles; no translator identified. One-fascicle scriptures:
forty-nine sections, ninety-eight fascicles. *Catalogue of Various Scriptures*, Fascicle Two. Mahāyāna: two hundred eighty-five sections, four hundred fascicles;
many translators identified. Multi-fascicle works: seventeen sections, one hundred twenty fascicles. No translator identified. Multi-fascicle works: two [sections].
Volume Three of the *Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of the Scriptures): Section One:
Seventeen volumes from five divisions, with one volume attributed to translators. Section Two: Fifty divisions and fifty volumes, with no translators credited.
Section Three: One volume. Section Four: Two hundred and thirteen divisions and two hundred and thirteen volumes.
In total, there are three hundred and sixty-two works comprising one thousand six hundred and eighty-two fascicles. First, the previously translated scriptures:

forty-five works in multiple fascicles (totaling two hundred seventy-nine fascicles), thirty-eight works in single fascicles (thirty-eight fascicles), twenty-nine works on Chan scriptures in multiple fascicles (thirty-eight fascicles), thirty-one works on Chan scriptures in single fascicles (thirty-one fascicles), and three [works] on the Vinaya.
Sixty-eight sections, two hundred and seventy-five fascicles:
Suspected Scriptures (462 sections, 67 fascicles);
Commentaries on Scriptures (50 sections, 246 fascicles); Numerical Treatises (6).
Commentaries on Meaning: 31 works, totaling 367 fascicles.
Section 7: Catalogue of Various Scriptures: 38 works, totaling 341 fascicles. Volume 4. Total:
129 works, totaling 985 fascicles. Part One: Individual Titles According to Subject Matter.
Thirteen collections totaling four hundred and thirteen fascicles, collectively titled according to their subject matter;
twenty-three collections totaling four hundred and seventy fascicles, consisting of parables;
and three collections totaling thirty-six fascicles, concerning the names of Buddhas.
The Catalogue of the Scriptures of the Great Sui Dynasty,
comprising a total of twenty items consisting of fourteen sections in nineteen fascicles of *shenzhou* (divine spells), fifty-four sections in forty-seven fascicles, and four general fascicles;
totaling one thousand four hundred and thirty-three sections in three thousand seven hundred and forty-one fascicles.

In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, by imperial decree, the twenty great virtuous ones (bhadanta) including Dharmakṣema and others compiled the *Catalogue of the Mahāyāna Sūtra Piṭaka* in six divisions, totaling seven hundred and eighty-four works in one thousand seven hundred and eighteen fascicles: The section on various sūtras translated once:
one hundred thirty-three works in four hundred and twenty-one fascicles; The section on various sūtras with multiple translations:
one hundred and ninety-five works in five hundred and thirty-two fascicles; The section on various sūtras of lost translation.
The Section on Various Derivatives of the Scriptures comprises one hundred thirty-four works in two hundred seventy-five fascicles;
the Section on Doubtful Scriptures comprises two hundred twenty-one works in two hundred sixty-four fascicles;
and the Section on Spurious Scriptures comprises twenty-one works in thirty fascicles.
The Catalogue of the Śrāvaka Sūtra Piṭaka (80 sections, 196 fascicles), Part II, Section 6; totaling 842 works in 1,201 fascicles:
the section of works translated by a single person (72 works, 292 fascicles);
the section of works with different translations (100 works, 270 fascicles); and the section of works of unknown translators.
The Section on Various Derivatives of the Scriptures consists of two hundred and fifty works totaling two hundred and seventy-two fascicles;
the Section on Doubtful Scriptures consists of three hundred and forty-one works totaling three hundred and forty-six fascicles;
and the Section on Spurious Scriptures consists of twenty-nine works totaling thirty-one fascicles.

The Catalogue of the Mahāyāna Vinaya Piṭaka consists of fifty-three sections totaling ninety-three fascicles, divided into three parts: the section on the Vinaya translated by a single person contains fifty sections totaling eighty-three fascicles;
the section on various Vinayas translated by different persons contains twelve sections totaling thirty-two fascicles;
and the section on various Vinayas of lost translations contains seven sections totaling seven fascicles.
The Section on the Separate Origins of the Various Vinayas comprises twelve divisions and fourteen fascicles;
the Section on Doubts Regarding the Various Vinayas comprises one division and two fascicles;
and the Section on Spurious and False [Vinayas].
The Combined Record of the Two Sections of the Eleven-Volume *Vinaya Piṭaka* of the Hīnayāna, Parts Four and Six, totaling sixty-two works in three hundred eighty-one fascicles;
the Section on Various Vinayas Translated by a Single Translator, totaling fifteen works in one hundred ninety-eight fascicles;
the Section on Various Vinayas with Different Translations, totaling eight works in one hundred twenty-six fascicles; and the Section on Various Vinayas of Lost Translation.
In total, there are twenty-nine sections comprising thirty-five fascicles:
the Section on the Various Derivatives of the Vinaya consists of six sections totaling six fascicles;
the Section on Doubts Regarding the Vinaya consists of two sections totaling three fascicles; and the Section on Spurious and False [Vinaya Texts].
The Tripiṭaka of Mahāyāna Abhidharma, combined in three divisions and three fascicles, totaling fifty-six sections and two hundred eighty-one fascicles;
the Section of Various Treatises Translated by a Single Translator, totaling forty-two sections and two hundred six fascicles;
the Section of Various Treatises with Different Translations, totaling eight sections and fifty-two fascicles; and the Section of Various Treatises of Lost Translation.
The Section on the Separate Origins of Various Treatises:
a total of fifteen works in nineteen fascicles; the Section on Doubts Concerning Various Treatises:
a total of one work in one fascicle; the Section on Spurious and False Treatises.

The Section of Combined Translations: one division, one fascicle; the Section of the Small Vehicle Abhidharma Piṭaka: six divisions, six sections, totaling one hundred and sixteen works in four hundred and eighty-two fascicles; the Section of Various Treatises Translated by a Single Translator:
one division, fourteen works, totaling two hundred and seventy-six fascicles; the Section of Various Treatises with Different Translations:
one division, eight works, totaling sixty-six fascicles; the Section of Various Treatises of Lost Translation.
The Section on the Separate Origins of Various Treatises, comprising five divisions and twenty-two fascicles;
the Section on Doubts Regarding Various Treatises, comprising one division and one fascicle;
and the Section on Spurious and False Treatises.

Combined into two divisions, ten fascicles: *The Collection Compiled after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*, seven divisions, totaling one hundred forty-four works in six hundred twenty-seven fascicles; *The Collection Compiled by Sages and Worthies of the Western Regions*, four divisions, totaling forty-eight works in one hundred nineteen fascicles;
*The Collection Compiled by Various Virtuous Masters of This Land*, nine divisions, totaling ninety-six works in five hundred eight fascicles;
*The Records of Transmission after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*, eight divisions, totaling two parts.

Combined, these comprise sixty-eight sections totaling one hundred eighty-five fascicles: the Section on the Biographies of Holy Sages of the Western Regions consists of thirteen sections totaling thirty fascicles;
the Section on the Biographies of Virtuous Masters of This Land consists of fifty-five sections totaling one hundred fifty-five fascicles;

and the Section on Works Composed after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa consists of ninety-two parts totaling one hundred nineteen sections and one hundred thirty-four fascicles. This concludes the Section on the Works Composed by Holy Sages of the Western Regions.

Combined, these comprise fifteen sections and nineteen fascicles. The writings produced by various virtuous masters of this land amount to one hundred and four sections and one hundred and fifteen fascicles.

The nine catalogs listed above total two thousand two hundred and fifty-seven sections and five thousand three hundred and ten fascicles; since these were all found through searching the records of the six previous families, the essential characteristics and applications of each family’s catalog are set forth as above.

The aforementioned single-fascicle catalog appears to be a list of scriptures brought by Śrīlaṅka and others during the Qin dynasty; however, the actual scriptures have not yet been seen. The single-fascicle "Catalog of Buddhist Scriptures from the Han Dynasty" appears to be a record compiled by Kāśyapa Mātanga immediately after he first translated the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*. The single-fascicle "Han Catalog" by Zhu Shixing and the single-fascicle "Old Catalog of the Wei Dynasty" appear to be records of scriptures seen by Liu Xiang while collecting the imperial library during the Former Han. The single-fascicle "Catalog of Shi Dao’an" dates to the Qin period.
One scroll of the *Niet Daozhen Lu* (Record of Niet Daozhen); one scroll of the *Shi Sengrui Erqin Lu* (Record of the Two Qin by the Monk Sengrui) from the Jin dynasty;

one scroll of the *Zhu Shixing Han Lu* (Han Record by Zhu Shixing) from the Later Qin; four scrolls of the *Zhu Daozu Zhongjing Lu* (Record of Various Scriptures by Zhu Daozu) from the Wei dynasty; one scroll of the *Hexi Weilu* (Spurious Record of Hexi); one scroll of the *Zhu Fahu Lu* (Record of Zhu Fahu);
one scroll of the *Zhi Mindu Lu* (Record of Zhi Mindu) from the Jin dynasty; and one scroll of the *Youdulu* (General Record of the Eastern Jin).
*Shi Wangzong Lu* (Record of Shi Wangzong), two fascicles; *Qian Qi Shi Shi Hongchong Lu* (Record of Monk Hongchong of the Former Qi Dynasty), one fascicle;
*Shi Daohui Song Qi Lu* (Record of Shi Daohui of the Song and Qi Dynasties), one fascicle; *Shi Daoping Lu* (Record of Shi Daoping), one fascicle;
*Shi Zhengdu Lu* (Record of Shi Zhengdu), one fascicle; *Wang Cheqi Lu* (Record of General Wang), one fascicle.
*Shixing lu* (Record of Initial Flourishing), one fascicle; *Lushan lu* (Record of Mount Lu), one fascicle;

*Zhao lu* (Record of the Zhao Period), one fascicle—these appear to be records from the time of the Zhao dynasty that raised doubts regarding the names and titles of those who had not yet seen the scriptures; *Cen hao lu* (Record of the Surname Cen), one fascicle;
*Bodhiruci lu* (Record of Bodhiruci), one fascicle; and *Houwei Shi Sengshao Hualin Fodian lu* (Record of the Hualin Buddhist Hall by the Monk Sengshao of the Later Wei), four fascicles.

In the fourteenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, an imperial edict commissioned the śramaṇa Shi Sengshao to compile one fascicle of the *Catalogue of Scriptures Translated by Dharma Master Lingyu* and eight fascicles of the *General Catalogue of All Scriptures*.

These appear to be composite works that synthesize the records of various schools; the authors are not detailed. To the right are the catalogues of twenty-four families, which have been verified through biographies and historical records.
Since these have not been previously encountered,
they are listed hereafter so that they may be transmitted for ten thousand generations. *Lidai Sanbao Ji*, Scroll Fifteen.
